lessons.theory: A container is a process (or group of processes) running on the host kernel, isolated so that it sees its own filesystem, network, and process tree. It is not a lightweight VM — there is no guest operating system and no hypervisor. A virtual machine virtualizes hardware: each VM ships a full guest OS kernel, and a hypervisor (KVM, ESXi, Hyper-V) emulates virtual hardware for it, which costs gigabytes of disk and seconds-to-minutes of boot time. A container instead shares the host's kernel and only packages the application plus its userspace dependencies (libraries, binaries, config). That is why a container starts in milliseconds and an image can be a few megabytes. The trade-off: because containers share the host kernel, they provide weaker isolation than VMs — a kernel exploit in one container can in principle affect the host, whereas a VM has a hardware boundary. In practice you often combine both: VMs for hard multi-tenant isolation, containers inside them for packaging and density.

examples.label: Run a container and see it is just a host process
examples.code:
# Start nginx in the background
docker run -d --name web nginx

# On the HOST, find the nginx process — it is a normal process
ps aux | grep nginx

# Its PID inside the container is 1, but on the host it is some large PID

examples.label: Container starts in milliseconds
examples.code:
time docker run --rm alpine echo "hello"
# real ~0.3s — no OS boot, just a process starting

tips: Think 'isolated process', not 'tiny VM' — it reframes most Docker behaviour correctly.
Containers are ephemeral by design: treat them as disposable and keep state in volumes or external services.
One concern per container (one app/process) makes scaling, logging, and restarts predictable.
gotchas: A Linux container image will not run a different kernel — you cannot run a Windows container on a Linux kernel or vice versa without a VM layer (this is what Docker Desktop quietly does on Mac/Windows).
'It works on my machine' isn't fully solved: the kernel is shared, so kernel-version-specific behaviour can still differ between hosts.
Because the kernel is shared, --privileged or a kernel CVE can break isolation. Containers are an isolation boundary, not a security sandbox by default.

lessons.theory: Containers are built from two native Linux kernel features. Namespaces provide isolation — they control what a process can see. There are several: PID (its own process tree, so the container's main process is PID 1), NET (its own network interfaces, routing table, and ports), MNT (its own filesystem mount points), UTS (its own hostname), IPC (its own shared-memory/semaphores), and USER (its own UID/GID mapping). cgroups (control groups) provide limitation — they control what a process can use: CPU shares, memory ceilings, block-IO bandwidth, and PID counts. Docker simply orchestrates these: when you run a container, the daemon asks the kernel to create a new set of namespaces and a cgroup, then starts your process inside them. Nothing about a container exists that you could not, in principle, set up by hand with unshare and the cgroup filesystem — Docker just makes it ergonomic and reproducible.

examples.label: See the namespaces a container gets
examples.code:
docker run -d --name demo nginx
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' demo)

# List the namespaces the kernel created for it
sudo ls -l /proc/$PID/ns
# -> net, pid, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup

examples.label: Apply a cgroup memory limit
examples.code:
# Cap memory at 256 MB; the kernel OOM-kills the process if it exceeds it
docker run -d --name limited --memory=256m nginx
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}' limited   # 268435456 bytes

examples.label: Create isolation by hand (what Docker automates)
examples.code:
# A new PID + mount namespace with a shell as 'PID 1'
sudo unshare --pid --mount --fork bash
echo $$   # 1

tips: Namespaces = visibility/isolation; cgroups = resource limits. Memorising that split explains almost every 'why can't my container see/use X' question.
Always set --memory and --cpus in production so one container can't starve its neighbours.
lsns on the host is a great way to inspect which namespaces exist and which PIDs share them.
gotchas: Without a memory cgroup limit, a container can consume all host RAM and take down everything else on the box.
By default containers share the host's USER namespace (root in the container maps to root on the host) — enable user-namespace remapping for stronger isolation.
PID 1 in a container has special signal-handling responsibilities; a process that doesn't reap children or handle SIGTERM leads to zombie processes and slow shutdowns (see tini / --init).

lessons.theory: A Docker image is not one blob — it is a stack of read-only layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile that changes the filesystem (FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD) produces a new layer containing just the diff from the previous one. At run time, Docker uses a union filesystem (OverlayFS on modern Linux) to merge those read-only layers into a single coherent view, then adds one thin writable layer on top for the running container. This is the storage driver. When a process inside the container writes to a file that lives in a lower read-only layer, OverlayFS performs copy-on-write: it copies the file up into the writable layer and edits the copy, leaving the image layer untouched. This is why images are shareable and space-efficient — ten containers from the same image share the identical read-only layers and each only pays for its own writable diff. It also explains why anything written into the writable layer disappears when the container is removed: that layer is discarded.

examples.label: Inspect the layers of an image
examples.code:
docker history node:20-alpine
# Each row is a layer, with the instruction that created it and its size

docker image inspect node:20-alpine -f '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}' | jq

examples.label: See copy-on-write in action
examples.code:
docker run --rm -it alpine sh
# inside: edit a file that came from the image
echo 'changed' >> /etc/hostname    # copied up to the writable layer
exit
# A fresh container from the same image is pristine again

examples.label: Where the layers live on disk
examples.code:
sudo ls /var/lib/docker/overlay2/
# lowerdir = image layers, upperdir = container writable layer, merged = the union view

tips: Order Dockerfile instructions from least- to most-frequently-changing so the expensive lower layers stay cached.
Each RUN/COPY/ADD is a layer — combine related commands with && to avoid layer sprawl, but keep cache-friendly boundaries.
Deleting a file in a later layer doesn't shrink the image: the data still exists in the lower layer (a 'whiteout' just hides it). Remove files in the same RUN that created them.
gotchas: Writing large amounts of data to the container's writable layer is slow (copy-on-write overhead) and lost on removal — use a volume for write-heavy workloads.
Secrets COPY'd in and then RUN-deleted are still recoverable from the earlier layer — never bake secrets, even temporarily.
The overlay2 driver needs a backing filesystem that supports it (ext4/xfs with ftype=1); misconfigured xfs is a classic 'driver failed' error.

lessons.theory: Docker is a client-server system, not a monolith. The Docker CLI (docker) is just a client: it sends REST calls over a Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock) or TCP to the Docker daemon (dockerd). The daemon is the long-running background service that does the real work — building images, managing networks and volumes, and supervising containers. But dockerd doesn't start containers directly. It hands off to containerd, a high-level container runtime that manages the container lifecycle and image pulls. containerd in turn spawns a low-level OCI runtime, runc, which is the small tool that actually talks to the kernel to create the namespaces and cgroups and exec your process. A per-container shim keeps the container running even if dockerd restarts. This layered design (CLI → dockerd → containerd → shim → runc) is why Kubernetes could drop the Docker daemon entirely and talk straight to containerd: the daemon is an orchestration convenience, not the thing that runs containers.

examples.label: The CLI just talks to the daemon's API
examples.code:
# This is what 'docker ps' does under the hood:
curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/containers/json | jq

examples.label: See the process tree of a running container
examples.code:
docker run -d --name web nginx
ps -ef --forest | grep -E 'dockerd|containerd|runc|nginx'
# dockerd -> containerd -> containerd-shim -> nginx

examples.label: Inspect the daemon
examples.code:
docker info        # daemon-wide config: storage driver, runtimes, cgroup version
docker version     # shows BOTH client and server (daemon) versions

tips: When 'Cannot connect to the Docker daemon' appears, the CLI is fine — the daemon (dockerd) isn't running or you lack socket permissions.
Add your user to the docker group to avoid sudo — but understand that's effectively root-equivalent access to the host.
Rootless mode runs the whole stack as an unprivileged user for much better security on shared hosts.
gotchas: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container gives that container full root control of the host — treat it as the most dangerous mount in Docker.
Client and daemon can be different versions; a too-new CLI against an old daemon throws API-version errors.
Killing dockerd does not necessarily kill running containers (thanks to the shim) — but it does stop you from managing them until it restarts.

lessons.theory: docker run is the workhorse, and it does several things in one shot: it pulls the image if it isn't local, creates a container from it, and starts the container. The flags you'll reach for constantly: -d (detached, run in the background), -it (interactive + TTY, for shells), --name (a stable name instead of a random one), -p HOST:CONTAINER (publish a port to the host), -e KEY=VALUE (set an environment variable), -v (mount a volume), and --rm (auto-remove the container when it exits, great for one-offs). The general shape is docker run [options] IMAGE [command] — anything after the image name overrides the image's default command. Understanding that run = pull + create + start also tells you the decomposition: docker create makes a container without starting it, and docker start runs an existing one, which is occasionally useful.

examples.label: The flags you'll use daily
examples.code:
# Detached web server, named, port published
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx
# visit http://localhost:8080

# Interactive throwaway shell
docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash

# Pass an environment variable
docker run --rm -e GREETING=hi alpine sh -c 'echo $GREETING'

examples.label: Override the default command
examples.code:
# nginx normally starts the server; here we run a shell instead
docker run --rm -it nginx bash

examples.label: run = create + start
examples.code:
docker create --name later nginx   # exists but not running
docker start later                  # now it runs

tips: Use --rm for any throwaway/debug container so you don't accumulate stopped containers.
-p HOST:CONTAINER is host-first — a very common mix-up. 8080:80 means 'host 8080 → container 80'.
Name your long-lived containers (--name) so scripts and docker exec are stable across restarts.
gotchas: Forgetting -d runs the container in the foreground and your terminal blocks until it exits.
EXPOSE in the image does NOT publish a port — you still need -p (or -P to publish all exposed ports to random host ports).
Container names must be unique; re-running with the same --name without removing the old one fails with a conflict.

lessons.theory: Once a container is running you'll frequently need to look inside it — to debug, inspect config, or check logs. docker exec runs a new process inside an already-running container; docker exec -it NAME sh (or bash) drops you into a shell. This is different from docker attach, which connects to the container's existing main process (PID 1) — useful occasionally but easy to accidentally kill the process with Ctrl-C. To inspect without entering, docker logs shows the container's stdout/stderr, docker inspect dumps its full JSON config (mounts, env, network, IP), docker top lists its processes, and docker diff shows files changed since the image. A key mental model: the shell you get from exec sees the container's merged union filesystem and its namespaces, so /etc, /app, and the process list are the container's, not the host's.

examples.label: Get a shell inside a running container
examples.code:
docker run -d --name web nginx
docker exec -it web bash      # explore /etc/nginx, /usr/share/nginx/html, etc.
# If bash isn't installed (alpine), use sh:
docker exec -it web sh

examples.label: Inspect without entering
examples.code:
docker logs web                       # stdout/stderr
docker inspect web | jq '.[0].NetworkSettings.IPAddress'
docker top web                        # processes inside
docker diff web                       # files changed vs the image

examples.label: Copy files in/out
examples.code:
docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./nginx.conf   # out
docker cp ./index.html web:/usr/share/nginx/html/  # in

tips: exec for a second process (debug shell), attach for the main process — prefer exec to avoid accidentally signalling PID 1.
Alpine-based images have sh but not bash — reach for sh first to avoid 'executable file not found'.
docker logs -f --tail 100 NAME is the fastest way to live-tail recent output.
gotchas: Ctrl-C while attached can send SIGINT to PID 1 and stop the container; detach with Ctrl-P Ctrl-Q instead.
Distroless or scratch images have NO shell at all — exec into them fails; debug with docker cp, docker inspect, or an ephemeral debug container sharing its namespaces.
Files you create via exec land in the throwaway writable layer and vanish when the container is removed.

lessons.t: FROM — choosing the right base image
lessons.theory: Every Dockerfile starts with FROM, which sets the base image all later layers build on. This single choice drives your image's size, attack surface, and which package manager and libc you get. The main families: full distros (ubuntu, debian) are large (~80–120 MB) but familiar and have every tool; -slim variants (debian:slim, python:3.12-slim) strip docs and extras for a fraction of the size; alpine images (~5–10 MB) are tiny but use musl libc instead of glibc, which occasionally breaks pre-compiled binaries; distroless images (gcr.io/distroless) contain only your app and its runtime — no shell, no package manager — for minimal attack surface; and scratch is the empty image, used for fully static binaries (common with Go). Always pin a specific tag (node:20.11-alpine, not node:latest) so builds are reproducible, and prefer official or verified-publisher images.

examples.label: Size differs enormously by base
examples.code:
FROM node:20            # ~380 MB
FROM node:20-slim       # ~70 MB
FROM node:20-alpine     # ~50 MB

examples.label: Pin a digest for full reproducibility
examples.code: FROM node:20-alpine@sha256:5b9e...   # exact bytes, immune to tag re-pushes

examples.label: scratch for a static Go binary
examples.code:
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
# ...build a static binary...
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

tips: Default to an -alpine or -slim tag and only move up if something breaks — you'll ship far smaller images.
Pin at least the minor version; pin the @sha256 digest for security-critical or compliance builds.
Prefer official images or Docker Verified Publisher images; random community images are a supply-chain risk.
gotchas: alpine uses musl libc — pre-built glibc binaries (some Node native modules, certain Python wheels) can fail with cryptic errors.
:latest is a moving target: a rebuild months later can silently pull a different OS and break you.
distroless and scratch have no shell, so you can't docker exec into them to debug — plan your debugging strategy up front.

lessons.theory: RUN executes a command during the build and commits the result as a new image layer. It has two forms: shell form (RUN apt-get update) runs through /bin/sh -c, and exec form (RUN ["executable","arg"]) runs the binary directly without a shell. Because each RUN is a separate layer, two principles matter. First, chain related commands with && in a single RUN so you don't create many thin layers and so cleanup happens in the same layer as the install (deleting cache in a later RUN doesn't shrink the image). Second, order RUNs so cache-stable steps come before frequently-changing ones. A canonical install line updates the package index, installs with --no-install-recommends, and removes the apt lists — all in one RUN.

examples.label: The canonical apt install (one layer, cleaned)
examples.code:
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl ca-certificates \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

examples.label: Shell vs exec form
examples.code:
RUN echo $HOME            # shell form — variable expands
RUN ["echo", "$HOME"]      # exec form — NO shell, prints the literal string

examples.label: Cache-busting on purpose
examples.code:
# Force a fresh install layer when needed
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl=7.88.*

tips: Combine update + install + cleanup in ONE RUN — splitting them creates stale-cache bugs and bloat.
Add --no-install-recommends (apt) and --no-cache-dir (pip) to skip dependencies and caches you don't need.
Use set -e (or rely on exec form) so a failing sub-command actually fails the build instead of being masked.
gotchas: 'apt-get update' in its own RUN, then 'install' in a later RUN, can install stale packages because the cached update layer is reused (the classic Docker cache trap).
Shell features ($VARS, pipes, &&) only work in shell form; exec form treats them as literal arguments.
rm -rf of caches in a separate RUN does NOT reduce image size — the data is already committed in the earlier layer.

lessons.theory: Both COPY and ADD move files from the build context into the image, but they differ in magic. COPY is literal and predictable: it copies files and directories, nothing more. ADD does everything COPY does plus two extra behaviours — it can fetch a remote URL, and it auto-extracts a local tar archive into the destination. Those conveniences are also footguns: a URL fetch isn't checksum-verified, and auto-extraction can surprise you. The official guidance is to use COPY by default and reach for ADD only when you specifically want local-tar extraction. For downloading remote files, prefer an explicit RUN curl with a checksum check over ADD, so the step is transparent and verifiable. Both honour .dockerignore and cache based on the contents of the files copied.

examples.label: Prefer COPY for plain copies
examples.code:
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
COPY src/ ./src/

examples.label: Legitimate ADD use: local tar auto-extract
examples.code: ADD release.tar.gz /opt/app/    # extracts the archive into /opt/app

examples.label: Download safely with RUN, not ADD
examples.code:
RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/tool.tgz -o /tmp/tool.tgz \
 && echo "<sha256>  /tmp/tool.tgz" | sha256sum -c - \
 && tar -xzf /tmp/tool.tgz -C /opt && rm /tmp/tool.tgz

tips: Rule of thumb: COPY unless you specifically need ADD's local-tar extraction.
Copy dependency manifests (package.json, requirements.txt) before the rest of the source to maximise cache reuse.
Use COPY --chown=user:group to set ownership in one step instead of a follow-up RUN chown.
gotchas: ADD with a URL gives no integrity check and breaks the build cache (it re-downloads), so you lose both safety and speed.
ADD auto-extracts local .tar files — if you actually wanted the tarball as a file, it'll silently unpack it.
COPY . . pulls in everything not excluded by .dockerignore — forgetting that file copies node_modules, .git, and secrets into the image.

lessons.theory: WORKDIR sets the working directory for any RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, or ADD that follows. If the directory doesn't exist, Docker creates it. It's the correct, persistent alternative to RUN cd: a cd inside a RUN only affects that one layer's shell and is forgotten by the next instruction, whereas WORKDIR persists for the rest of the build and becomes the container's default directory at runtime. You can use it multiple times and relative paths stack. Using an absolute path like /app keeps things predictable, and setting WORKDIR before COPY lets you copy into a clean, known location.

examples.label: WORKDIR persists; cd does not
examples.code:
WORKDIR /app          # all later steps run here, and it's created if missing
COPY . .              # copies into /app
RUN npm ci            # runs in /app

examples.label: The anti-pattern it replaces
examples.code:
# WRONG: cd doesn't carry to the next layer
RUN cd /app           # has no lasting effect
RUN npm ci            # runs in / , not /app

examples.label: Relative WORKDIRs stack
examples.code:
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR src           # now /app/src

tips: Always set an absolute WORKDIR early (e.g. /app) so the rest of the Dockerfile is unambiguous.
WORKDIR creates the directory for you — no need for RUN mkdir -p.
It also sets the runtime working directory, which simplifies your CMD paths.
gotchas: RUN cd somewhere is a no-op for later instructions — a very common beginner bug that WORKDIR fixes.
Building under / (no WORKDIR) clutters the root filesystem and makes COPY destinations error-prone.
A relative WORKDIR depends on the previous one; mixing absolute and relative can land you somewhere unexpected.

lessons.theory: ENV and ARG both define variables but live in different phases. ARG is build-time only: you declare it in the Dockerfile and can override it with docker build --build-arg NAME=value. It's gone once the image is built and is not available at runtime. ENV sets an environment variable that is baked into the image and present both during the rest of the build and at container runtime. A common pattern is to declare an ARG and use it to set a default ENV. Crucially, neither is a safe place for secrets: ARG values can appear in build history/logs, and ENV values are visible in docker inspect and to every process in the container. For secrets, use BuildKit's --secret mount (build-time) or runtime injection (--env-file, orchestrator secrets).

examples.label: ARG (build) vs ENV (runtime)
examples.code:
ARG NODE_VERSION=20          # build-time, overridable
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine

ENV NODE_ENV=production      # persists into the running container
ENV PORT=3000

examples.label: Override an ARG at build
examples.code: docker build --build-arg NODE_VERSION=18 -t app .

examples.label: ARG feeding an ENV default
examples.code:
ARG APP_PORT=8080
ENV PORT=${APP_PORT}

tips: Use ARG for things that only matter while building (versions, build flags); use ENV for runtime config.
Declare ARG before the FROM that uses it if you want to parameterise the base image tag.
Provide sensible ENV defaults so the image runs without requiring every variable to be set.
gotchas: Secrets in ARG leak into image history and CI logs; secrets in ENV are visible via docker inspect — never put credentials in either.
An ARG declared before FROM is out of scope after FROM unless you re-declare it in the build stage.
ENV values defined later can shadow earlier ones; and unlike RUN, ENV assignments aren't shell-evaluated the way you might expect.

lessons.theory: Both define what runs when the container starts, but they compose differently. ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable — the thing the container always runs. CMD sets the default arguments (or the default command if there's no ENTRYPOINT), and is easily overridden at docker run. The powerful pattern is ENTRYPOINT ["executable"] + CMD ["default-arg"]: the container behaves like that executable, and anything you append on docker run replaces CMD as its arguments. Always prefer the exec form (JSON array) over shell form: exec form makes your process PID 1 directly, so it receives signals like SIGTERM and shuts down cleanly; shell form wraps it in /bin/sh -c, which swallows signals and leads to 10-second kill timeouts.

examples.label: The classic ENTRYPOINT + CMD pattern
examples.code:
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]
CMD ["--port", "8000"]
# docker run img            -> python app.py --port 8000
# docker run img --port 9000 -> python app.py --port 9000

examples.label: Exec form forwards signals (use this)
examples.code:
CMD ["node", "server.js"]        # node is PID 1, gets SIGTERM
# NOT: CMD node server.js          # /bin/sh is PID 1, node ignores SIGTERM

examples.label: CMD alone (simple default command)
examples.code: CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

tips: ENTRYPOINT = what always runs; CMD = default args that are easy to override. Combine them for flexible images.
Always use exec (JSON-array) form so your app is PID 1 and handles SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.
An entrypoint.sh wrapper script (with exec "$@" at the end) is a clean way to do startup setup then hand off.
gotchas: Shell-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT makes /bin/sh PID 1; your app never sees SIGTERM and Docker hard-kills it after the grace period.
Only the LAST CMD (or ENTRYPOINT) in a Dockerfile takes effect — earlier ones are ignored.
If your entrypoint script doesn't end with exec "$@", signals won't reach your real process and you'll have zombie/slow-shutdown issues.

lessons.theory: EXPOSE is documentation, not action. It records which ports the application inside the container listens on, as metadata in the image. It does NOT publish the port to the host — that's the job of docker run -p HOST:CONTAINER (or -P to publish all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports). So why use it? It signals intent to anyone reading the Dockerfile or running docker inspect, it enables docker run -P, and orchestrators and tools can read it. Think of EXPOSE as a comment with teeth: it tells the human and the tooling 'this container serves on port 3000', while -p is what actually opens the door from the outside world.

examples.label: Document, then publish separately
examples.code:
# In the Dockerfile:
EXPOSE 3000

# At run time you STILL need -p to reach it:
docker run -p 8080:3000 myapp   # host 8080 -> container 3000

examples.label: Publish all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports
examples.code:
docker run -P myapp
docker port <container>   # see which host ports were assigned

examples.label: Container-to-container needs neither
examples.code:
# On the same Docker network, services reach each other on the container
# port directly (e.g. app -> db:5432) without EXPOSE or -p.

tips: Add EXPOSE for every port your app listens on — it's free documentation and enables -P.
Remember the actual exposure happens with -p at run time or ports: in compose.
On a user-defined network, containers talk on container ports directly — you don't publish internal-only services to the host.
gotchas: Beginners expect EXPOSE to make a port reachable from the host — it doesn't; without -p you'll get connection refused.
Publishing a database port to 0.0.0.0 exposes it to the whole network — bind to 127.0.0.1 or keep it internal.
EXPOSE the port your app actually binds to; mismatches (app on 8080, EXPOSE 3000) cause confusing -P mappings.

lessons.theory: docker build turns a Dockerfile + build context into an image. The context is the directory you point it at (usually .), and everything in it (minus .dockerignore entries) is sent to the daemon — so a bloated context slows every build. Tagging with -t name:tag gives the image a human name; an image can carry multiple tags. Good tagging discipline separates a moving tag like :latest or :main from immutable tags like a semantic version (:1.4.2) or a git SHA (:sha-abc1234), so deployments are traceable and reproducible. -f lets you point at a non-default Dockerfile, and --build-arg passes ARGs. With BuildKit (default in modern Docker) builds are faster and support advanced cache and secret features.

examples.label: Build and tag
examples.code:
docker build -t myapp:1.4.2 -t myapp:latest .
docker images myapp

examples.label: Custom Dockerfile + build arg
examples.code: docker build -f Dockerfile.prod --build-arg NODE_VERSION=20 -t myapp:prod .

examples.label: Tag for a registry and push
examples.code:
docker tag myapp:1.4.2 ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp:1.4.2
docker push ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp:1.4.2

tips: Tag with an immutable identifier (semver or git SHA) for anything you deploy — :latest alone makes rollbacks and audits painful.
Keep the build context small with a good .dockerignore; it speeds up every build and shrinks images.
Use docker build --progress=plain to see full output when debugging a failing layer.
gotchas: A huge build context (node_modules, .git, large data dirs) is uploaded to the daemon on every build — exclude it via .dockerignore.
Relying only on :latest means two machines can run different code under the same tag — always pin in production.
The build context is the directory argument, not where the Dockerfile lives; COPY paths are relative to the context root, not the Dockerfile.

lessons.theory: An image is an ordered stack of read-only layers, each the filesystem diff produced by one Dockerfile instruction (FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD). Layers are content-addressed by a SHA digest, which has two big consequences. First, identical layers are shared across images and cached locally, so pulling a new image that shares a base only downloads the layers you don't already have. Second, a layer's digest depends on its contents and on every layer below it — change one early layer and every layer after it is invalidated. Understanding layers is the foundation of every optimisation technique: caching, ordering, multi-stage builds, and size reduction all flow from 'what is in each layer and when does it change'.

examples.label: Inspect layers and their sizes
examples.code:
docker history --no-trunc myapp:latest
# Each row = a layer + the instruction + size it added

examples.label: Shared layers download once
examples.code:
docker pull node:20-alpine
docker pull node:20-alpine-with-app   # only the app layers download; base is reused

examples.label: A tool to visualise layer waste
examples.code:
# dive (https://github.com/wagoodman/dive)
dive myapp:latest   # shows wasted space and per-layer file changes

tips: Put rarely-changing instructions (base, system deps) early and frequently-changing ones (your source) late.
Use 'dive' or 'docker history' to find which layer is bloating your image.
Shared base layers across your images save real bandwidth and disk — standardise on a small set of bases.
gotchas: Removing a file in a later layer doesn't reclaim its space — the bytes persist in the earlier layer behind a whiteout.
Changing an early instruction invalidates the cache for everything after it, forcing a full rebuild from that point.
Each RUN/COPY/ADD is a layer; dozens of tiny RUNs create overhead and a hard-to-read history.

lessons.theory: Docker caches each layer and reuses it on the next build if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged. The cache is sequential: once one layer is a cache miss, every layer after it rebuilds. The optimisation, therefore, is to order instructions so the things that rarely change sit above the things that change every commit. The canonical example is dependency installation: copy only your dependency manifest (package.json, requirements.txt, go.mod) first, install dependencies, and only then copy the rest of the source. That way editing application code doesn't bust the expensive 'install dependencies' layer — Docker reuses it and your builds stay fast. Copying all source before installing dependencies is the single most common cause of slow rebuilds.

examples.label: Cache-friendly Node ordering
examples.code:
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./      # changes rarely
RUN npm ci                 # cached unless deps change
COPY . .                   # changes often, but doesn't re-trigger npm ci

examples.label: The slow anti-pattern
examples.code:
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .                   # ANY code change busts the cache here
RUN npm ci                 # re-runs on every commit — slow

examples.label: Python equivalent
examples.code:
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

tips: Copy the dependency manifest and install BEFORE copying source — the highest-leverage build-speed fix there is.
Keep a stable .dockerignore so unrelated files (logs, .git) don't invalidate COPY layers.
In CI, use --cache-from / registry cache so cache survives across ephemeral runners.
gotchas: COPY . . before installing dependencies means every source edit reinstalls everything — death by a thousand rebuilds.
A cache miss cascades: one changed early layer rebuilds all subsequent layers.
Timestamps or generated files in the context can silently bust COPY caches — exclude them via .dockerignore.

lessons.theory: A multi-stage build uses several FROM statements in one Dockerfile. Earlier stages do the heavy lifting — compiling code, installing build toolchains, running bundlers — and the final stage starts from a small base and copies in only the finished artifacts with COPY --from=<stage>. The build tools, compilers, dev dependencies, and intermediate files stay behind in the discarded builder stage and never reach your shipped image. This routinely cuts image size by 60–90% and shrinks the attack surface because the runtime image contains no compilers or package managers. You can name stages (FROM ... AS build), copy from earlier stages or even from external images, and target a specific stage with docker build --target.

examples.label: Node: build stage + slim runtime
examples.code:
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

examples.label: Go: builder + scratch (tiny)
examples.code:
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags='-s -w' -o /app .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]   # final image is just your binary

examples.label: Build only up to a stage
examples.code: docker build --target build -t myapp:builder .

tips: Name your stages (AS build) and copy only the artifacts you need into a minimal final base.
Put tests in an intermediate stage so a failing test fails the build, without shipping test tooling.
Use --target to stop at the builder stage for debugging or to share a dependency-cache stage.
gotchas: Forgetting COPY --from and copying the whole builder defeats the purpose — only copy the finished artifacts.
Paths in COPY --from are relative to that stage's filesystem; a wrong path silently copies nothing or errors.
Native modules built in the builder stage must be ABI-compatible with the runtime base (same libc/arch).

lessons.theory: Picking a smaller base is the easiest large win. -slim Debian variants drop documentation, locales, and extra tooling, cutting tens to a hundred-plus megabytes while keeping glibc and apt. alpine goes further with a ~5 MB base built on musl libc and the apk package manager. distroless images contain only your language runtime and your app — no shell, no package manager — minimising both size and attack surface. The trade-offs: alpine's musl libc and different DNS resolver behaviour can break glibc-compiled binaries or surface subtle networking differences; distroless and scratch can't be docker exec'd into for debugging. Choose the smallest base your app actually works on, and validate it under load, not just at build time.

examples.label: Same app, three bases
examples.code:
FROM python:3.12         # ~340 MB
FROM python:3.12-slim    # ~45 MB
FROM python:3.12-alpine  # ~50 MB (but musl — watch native wheels)

examples.label: Distroless runtime for Java
examples.code:
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
# ...build the jar...
FROM gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12
COPY --from=build /app/app.jar /app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]

examples.label: Compare final sizes
examples.code: docker images | grep myapp

tips: Start from -slim or -alpine; only move to a fuller base if you hit a real incompatibility.
For compiled languages, pair a builder image with distroless or scratch for a tiny, hardened runtime.
Measure with docker images and test the running app — size isn't worth a subtle runtime break.
gotchas: alpine's musl libc breaks some prebuilt binaries and certain Python/Node native packages — you may need to compile from source.
alpine's DNS resolver has historically behaved differently from glibc, causing intermittent resolution issues in some setups.
distroless/scratch have no shell — you can't exec in; debug with ephemeral sidecar containers or docker cp instead.

lessons.theory: .dockerignore works like .gitignore but for the build context: it lists files and directories that should NOT be sent to the Docker daemon when you build. This matters for three reasons. Speed: the entire context is uploaded to the daemon before the build starts, so excluding node_modules, .git, build artifacts, and large data folders makes builds noticeably faster. Size and cache: it prevents irrelevant files from busting COPY caches and from accidentally bloating images via COPY . .. Security: it stops secrets, .env files, SSH keys, and credentials from being copied into image layers. A good .dockerignore is short but high-impact, and every project that uses COPY . . should have one.

examples.label: A solid baseline .dockerignore
examples.code:
.git
node_modules
npm-debug.log
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
.env
*.md
dist
coverage
.vscode

examples.label: Why it matters with COPY . .
examples.code:
# Without .dockerignore this copies .git, node_modules, .env into the image:
COPY . .
# With .dockerignore those are excluded automatically.

examples.label: Patterns support negation
examples.code:
*
!src
!package.json   # ignore everything, then explicitly include what you need

tips: Always exclude .git, node_modules (rebuild inside the image), .env, and local caches.
Add a .dockerignore even for small projects — it prevents accidental secret leakage via COPY . .
Use the allowlist pattern (* then !needed) when you want tight control over what enters the context.
gotchas: No .dockerignore + COPY . . is the classic way secrets and 500 MB of node_modules end up baked into an image.
.dockerignore is read from the build-context root, not next to the Dockerfile if they differ.
It only affects the build context (COPY/ADD); it doesn't remove files that a RUN command generates.

lessons.t: Analyzing image size with docker history
lessons.theory: When an image is bigger than expected, you need to find which layer is responsible. docker history IMAGE lists every layer with the instruction that created it and the size it contributed — read it top-down to spot the heavy hitters (a forgotten cache, an unremoved build dependency, a large COPY). For a deeper, file-level view, the open-source tool dive shows each layer's exact file changes and estimates wasted space (files added then deleted, duplicate content). docker image inspect exposes the raw layer digests and total size as JSON. The workflow is: history to locate the fat layer, dive to see what's inside it, then fix the Dockerfile (combine RUNs, clean caches, move work into a builder stage).

examples.label: Find the heavy layers
examples.code:
docker history myapp:latest
# Look for big SIZE values and the instruction that caused them

examples.label: File-level analysis with dive
examples.code:
dive myapp:latest
# Shows per-layer file tree, wasted space, and an efficiency score

examples.label: Total size and layer digests
examples.code:
docker image inspect myapp:latest -f '{{.Size}}'
docker image inspect myapp:latest -f '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}' | jq

tips: Use docker history first to localise the problem, then dive to see the offending files.
Watch for 'install build tools' layers that should live in a discarded builder stage.
Track image size in CI and fail the build if it regresses past a threshold.
gotchas: history shows sizes per layer, but space removed in a later layer still counts in the earlier one — the diff can be misleading.
Squashing layers hides history and can hurt cache sharing; prefer fixing the Dockerfile over --squash.
A small compressed size on a registry can still be a large uncompressed size at runtime — measure the on-disk size.

lessons.theory: BuildKit is Docker's modern build engine (default in current Docker). It builds independent stages in parallel, has a smarter and more granular cache, supports remote cache import/export for CI, and adds two features that solve real problems: secret mounts and cache mounts. A secret mount (RUN --mount=type=secret) exposes a credential to a single RUN command without ever writing it into a layer — perfect for private package registries or build-time tokens, which ARG and ENV would leak. A cache mount (RUN --mount=type=cache) persists a package-manager cache (npm, pip, apt, go) across builds without baking it into the image, dramatically speeding repeat builds. Enable secret syntax with a # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 header.

examples.label: Build-time secret that never lands in a layer
examples.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:20-alpine
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmtoken \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npmtoken) npm ci
# build with:
# docker build --secret id=npmtoken,src=$HOME/.npmtoken -t app .

examples.label: Cache mount speeds repeat installs
examples.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci

examples.label: Export/import cache in CI
examples.code:
docker buildx build \
  --cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/eknatha/app:cache \
  --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/eknatha/app:cache \
  -t ghcr.io/eknatha/app:ci .

tips: Use --mount=type=secret for any build-time credential — it's the only way to avoid leaking it into image history.
Use --mount=type=cache for package managers to make repeated builds fast without bloating the image.
Add the '# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1' header to unlock the newest Dockerfile features.
gotchas: ARG/ENV-based 'secrets' persist in image history forever — BuildKit secret mounts exist precisely to avoid that.
Secret and cache mount syntax requires BuildKit and the syntax header; without them the build errors or ignores the mount.
Cache mounts are local to the builder; in ephemeral CI you also need registry cache (--cache-to/--cache-from) to persist them.

lessons.theory: Bridge is the default network driver for standalone containers. When the daemon starts it creates a virtual bridge called docker0; each container gets a virtual ethernet pair connecting it to that bridge and a private IP (typically in 172.17.0.0/16). Containers on the bridge can reach the outside world through NAT (the host masquerades their traffic), and the host can reach them by IP. There's an important distinction: the default bridge (docker0) does NOT provide name-based service discovery — containers can only find each other by IP or the legacy --link. A user-defined bridge (one you create with docker network create) DOES provide automatic DNS, so containers resolve each other by name, and it isolates its members from containers on other networks. Best practice is to always use a user-defined bridge rather than the default.

examples.label: Create and use a user-defined bridge
examples.code:
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:15
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapi
# 'api' can now reach the database at hostname 'db'

examples.label: Inspect the bridge and its members
examples.code:
docker network inspect appnet
docker network inspect bridge -f '{{json .Containers}}' | jq

examples.label: Default bridge has no DNS
examples.code:
docker run -d --name a busybox sleep 1d
docker run --rm busybox ping -c1 a   # fails by name on the default bridge

tips: Always create a user-defined bridge (docker network create) — you get DNS by name and network isolation for free.
Compose creates a user-defined bridge automatically, which is why service-name DNS 'just works' there.
Put related services on the same network and unrelated ones on separate networks to limit blast radius.
gotchas: The default 'bridge' network gives no automatic name resolution — a frequent source of 'why can't my containers find each other'.
docker0's 172.17.x.x subnet can collide with corporate/VPN subnets; change it in daemon.json if you see routing weirdness.
Container IPs are ephemeral — never hardcode them; rely on DNS names on a user-defined network.

lessons.t: Host networking — when to use it
lessons.theory: With --network host the container skips its own network namespace and shares the host's network stack directly. There's no NAT and no port mapping — if the app listens on 8080, it's on the host's 8080 immediately. The upside is the lowest possible latency and no per-packet NAT overhead, which matters for high-throughput or latency-sensitive workloads and for tools that need to see the host's real interfaces. The downsides are significant: zero network isolation between the container and host, direct port conflicts with host services, and reduced portability. Host networking is also Linux-only — on Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows) it doesn't behave the same because containers run inside a VM. Reach for it deliberately, not by default.

examples.label: Run with host networking
examples.code:
docker run -d --network host nginx
# nginx is reachable on the HOST's port 80 directly — no -p needed

examples.label: No -p flag has any effect
examples.code:
docker run --network host -p 8080:80 nginx
# the -p is ignored; the container uses host ports as-is

examples.label: When it helps: a network monitoring tool
examples.code: docker run --rm --network host nicolaka/netshoot tcpdump -i eth0

tips: Use host mode for latency-critical apps or tools that must see the host's real interfaces.
Confirm there are no port clashes with existing host services before switching.
On Mac/Windows, expect different behaviour — host networking is a Linux-kernel feature.
gotchas: No isolation: a compromised container in host mode has direct access to the host network — a real security cost.
-p port publishing is meaningless in host mode; the app binds host ports directly and can collide.
Two host-network containers can't both bind the same port — they fight over the host's single port space.

lessons.theory: Containers on the same user-defined network talk to each other directly using the container/service name as the hostname and the target's container port — no host port publishing required. So an 'api' container connects to a database simply as db:5432, and a cache as redis:6379. The traffic never leaves the Docker network, so you do NOT need (and shouldn't use) -p for purely internal services; publishing a database to the host just widens the attack surface. Containers on different networks are isolated and can't reach each other unless you attach a container to multiple networks (a common pattern for a gateway/proxy that needs to talk to both a frontend and a backend network). The mental model: same network = reachable by name on the container port; different network = isolated.

examples.label: API talks to DB by name, no published port
examples.code:
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=x postgres:15
docker run -d --name api --network appnet -e DB_HOST=db -e DB_PORT=5432 myapi
# api connects to db:5432 internally; db is NOT exposed to the host

examples.label: Multi-network gateway pattern
examples.code:
docker network create frontend
docker network create backend
docker run -d --name proxy --network frontend nginx
docker network connect backend proxy   # proxy now bridges both

examples.label: Test connectivity between containers
examples.code: docker run --rm --network appnet busybox ping -c1 db

tips: Reference other services by name on their container port — don't publish internal services to the host.
Attach a proxy/gateway to multiple networks to mediate between isolated tiers.
Use nicolaka/netshoot on the same network to debug connectivity (dig, curl, nc, tcpdump).
gotchas: Containers on different networks can't see each other — forgetting to put them on the same network causes 'connection refused'.
Publishing a DB with -p just to let another container reach it is wrong and insecure — same-network name resolution is the answer.
Using localhost from one container to reach another fails: localhost is the container itself, not its neighbour.

lessons.theory: On a user-defined network, Docker runs an embedded DNS server at the fixed address 127.0.0.11 inside each container. When your app resolves a name like db, the container's resolver queries 127.0.0.11, which maps the service/container name to its current IP — and updates automatically if the container restarts with a new IP. This is what makes service-name connectivity reliable: you never deal with IPs. In Docker Compose, the service name is the DNS name, and Compose puts all services on one auto-created user-defined network, so app -> db:5432 works out of the box. Names that the embedded DNS doesn't know (external domains) are forwarded to the host's upstream DNS. You can add aliases, and on the default bridge none of this applies — only user-defined networks get the embedded DNS.

examples.label: Service name resolves via embedded DNS
examples.code:
# docker-compose.yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb  # 'db' resolves
  db:
    image: postgres:15

examples.label: See the embedded resolver
examples.code:
docker run --rm --network appnet busybox cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 127.0.0.11

examples.label: Add a network alias
examples.code:
docker run -d --name db --network appnet \
  --network-alias database postgres:15
# reachable as both 'db' and 'database'

tips: Use service/container names as hostnames; let Docker's DNS handle the changing IPs.
In Compose, the service key IS the DNS name — keep them meaningful (db, redis, api).
Set custom upstream DNS with --dns if external resolution fails inside containers.
gotchas: Embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) only exists on user-defined networks — the default bridge can't resolve names.
Resolving a service before it's started yields a failure; pair with depends_on + healthchecks and app-level retries.
Some alpine/musl resolver quirks have caused intermittent lookups — test name resolution under your real base image.

lessons.theory: docker network create makes a user-defined network you fully control: its driver (bridge for single-host, overlay for multi-host), its subnet and gateway, and which containers attach to it. Custom networks are the recommended default because they give automatic DNS, isolation from other networks, and the ability to segment an application into tiers (e.g. a public 'frontend' network and a private 'backend' network so the database is unreachable from the edge). You can attach a container at run time (--network) or later (docker network connect), and a single container can live on several networks at once. Managing networks explicitly — rather than dumping everything on the default bridge — is a core part of designing secure, understandable container topologies.

examples.label: Create with a custom subnet
examples.code:
docker network create --driver bridge \
  --subnet 10.10.0.0/24 --gateway 10.10.0.1 appnet

examples.label: Segment frontend and backend tiers
examples.code:
docker network create frontend
docker network create backend
docker run -d --name web   --network frontend nginx
docker run -d --name db    --network backend  postgres:15
docker run -d --name api   --network backend  myapi
docker network connect frontend api   # api bridges both tiers

examples.label: Manage networks
examples.code:
docker network ls
docker network inspect backend
docker network rm appnet   # only when no containers are attached

tips: Design networks around trust tiers — keep databases on a backend network unreachable from the public edge.
Name networks by role (frontend/backend/data) so the topology reads clearly.
Use docker network connect/disconnect to attach gateways and proxies to multiple tiers.
gotchas: Custom subnets can collide with host/VPN ranges — pick ranges that don't overlap your environment.
You can't remove a network while containers are still attached — disconnect or stop them first.
Putting everything on one network defeats isolation; segment so a breach in one tier doesn't reach the data tier.

lessons.theory: Bridge networks are single-host. To let containers on different physical machines communicate as if on one network, Docker uses the overlay driver. Overlay networks encapsulate container traffic in VXLAN tunnels over the hosts' physical network, presenting a flat layer-2 network that spans the cluster. They are the foundation of Docker Swarm's multi-host service discovery and load balancing, and the same concept underpins Kubernetes CNI plugins. Setting up an overlay requires a key-value store or Swarm mode to coordinate the hosts. For most single-node development you'll never need overlay — but understanding it is essential for orchestration, where services on many nodes must find and talk to each other seamlessly.

examples.label: Create an overlay in Swarm
examples.code:
docker swarm init                       # on the manager node
docker network create -d overlay appnet
docker service create --name api --network appnet myapi

examples.label: Attachable overlay for standalone containers
examples.code:
docker network create -d overlay --attachable appnet
# standalone containers (not just services) can now join it

examples.label: Inspect overlay scope
examples.code: docker network inspect appnet -f '{{.Scope}}'   # swarm

tips: Overlay is for multi-host/orchestration — don't reach for it on a single dev machine.
Use --attachable if you need plain containers (not Swarm services) on the overlay.
Understand overlay conceptually before Kubernetes — CNI networking is the same flat-network idea.
gotchas: Overlay needs Swarm mode or an external KV store to coordinate hosts — it won't work standalone without setup.
VXLAN uses UDP 4789 and control ports (7946, 2377); firewalls blocking them silently break overlay traffic.
Added encapsulation means a slightly smaller effective MTU — large packets can fragment or drop if MTU isn't tuned.

lessons.theory: Publishing a port is what actually makes a container reachable from outside the Docker network. The flag is -p HOST:CONTAINER (host port first — a frequent mix-up), e.g. -p 8080:80 maps host 8080 to container 80. You can bind to a specific host interface (-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 to expose only on localhost), pick a protocol (-p 53:53/udp), or let Docker assign random host ports with -P (which publishes every EXPOSEd port). EXPOSE alone publishes nothing — it's just metadata. The key decisions: only publish ports that truly need host/external access, and bind sensitive services to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0 so they aren't exposed to the whole network.

examples.label: Map and bind to localhost only
examples.code:
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 postgres:15
# Postgres reachable only from the host itself, not the LAN

examples.label: Random host ports with -P
examples.code:
docker run -d -P nginx
docker port <container>   # see which host ports were assigned

examples.label: UDP and specific interface
examples.code: docker run -d -p 192.168.1.10:53:53/udp coredns

tips: Remember -p is host:container — getting the order wrong publishes the wrong port.
Bind databases and admin ports to 127.0.0.1 so they aren't exposed beyond the host.
Use -P during quick experiments; use explicit -p with fixed ports in anything reproducible.
gotchas: -p 0.0.0.0:5432:5432 (the default 0.0.0.0) exposes the service to your entire network — often unintended for databases.
Publishing a port already in use on the host fails with 'address already in use'.
EXPOSE without -p means the port is documented but not reachable from the host — connection refused.

lessons.theory: Sometimes a container needs to look like a real device on the physical LAN — its own MAC and a routable IP in your existing subnet — for example, legacy applications that expect direct network presence, or services that must be reachable without port mapping. macvlan gives each container a unique MAC address on the parent interface, so the network sees it as a separate physical host. ipvlan is similar but shares the parent's MAC and differentiates by IP (L2 mode) or routes (L3 mode), which suits environments where switches limit the number of MACs per port. Both require the parent NIC in promiscuous mode (for macvlan) and careful IP/subnet planning to avoid clashes with DHCP. They're powerful but niche — most workloads are better served by bridge or overlay.

examples.label: Create a macvlan network
examples.code:
docker network create -d macvlan \
  --subnet 192.168.1.0/24 --gateway 192.168.1.1 \
  -o parent=eth0 lan
docker run -d --network lan --ip 192.168.1.50 --name legacy myapp
# container is reachable at 192.168.1.50 on the physical LAN

examples.label: ipvlan L2 mode
examples.code:
docker network create -d ipvlan \
  --subnet 192.168.1.0/24 -o parent=eth0 -o ipvlan_mode=l2 lan2

examples.label: Reserve a range to avoid DHCP clashes
examples.code:
docker network create -d macvlan \
  --subnet 192.168.1.0/24 --ip-range 192.168.1.192/27 \
  -o parent=eth0 lan

tips: Use macvlan/ipvlan only when a container genuinely needs to be a first-class device on the physical network.
Carve out an --ip-range outside your DHCP pool to prevent address conflicts.
Prefer ipvlan where switch security limits MACs per port, or where promiscuous mode isn't allowed.
gotchas: By default the host can't talk to its own macvlan containers — that requires an extra macvlan sub-interface on the host.
macvlan needs promiscuous mode on the parent NIC, which many cloud providers and some switches forbid.
Hand out IPs carefully — overlapping with DHCP-assigned addresses causes intermittent, hard-to-debug conflicts.

lessons.theory: A running container's filesystem is the image's read-only layers plus a single thin writable layer on top, merged by the storage driver (OverlayFS). Anything a process writes goes into that writable layer using copy-on-write. The defining property: that writable layer is tied to the container's lifecycle — remove the container and the layer, and all data written to it, is gone. This is by design; containers are meant to be disposable and stateless. It's also why writing large or frequently-changing data to the container filesystem is both slow (copy-on-write overhead) and dangerous (lost on removal). The solution to persistence is to mount storage that lives outside the writable layer — volumes, bind mounts, or tmpfs — which is the subject of this module.

examples.label: Data in the writable layer is lost on removal
examples.code:
docker run --name tmp alpine sh -c 'echo hi > /data.txt'
docker rm tmp
# /data.txt is gone forever — it lived only in the writable layer

examples.label: See changes vs the image
examples.code:
docker run -d --name web nginx
docker exec web sh -c 'echo test > /tmp/x'
docker diff web   # A /tmp/x  (added in the writable layer)

examples.label: Writable layer is per-container
examples.code:
# Two containers from one image have independent writable layers
docker run -d --name a nginx
docker run -d --name b nginx   # a's changes never affect b

tips: Treat the container filesystem as scratch space — anything you must keep goes in a volume.
Keep write-heavy paths (databases, uploads, logs) on volumes to avoid copy-on-write slowness.
Design apps to be stateless so containers can be killed and recreated freely.
gotchas: docker rm deletes the writable layer and its data — a leading cause of accidental data loss.
Heavy writes to the container layer are slow and can fill the host's Docker storage area.
Restarting a container keeps its writable layer, but recreating it (new container) does not — know the difference.

lessons.t: Named volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs
lessons.theory: Docker offers three mount types. Named volumes are managed by Docker, stored under /var/lib/docker/volumes, and are the recommended choice for persistent application data (databases, uploads): they're portable, easy to back up, and decoupled from the host's directory layout. Bind mounts map a specific host path into the container; they're ideal for development (live-editing source code on the host and seeing changes instantly) but tie you to the host's filesystem and can introduce permission and portability issues. tmpfs mounts store data in the host's RAM only — nothing is written to disk — which suits sensitive secrets or fast scratch space that should vanish when the container stops. The modern --mount syntax is explicit and preferred over the older -v shorthand.

examples.label: Named volume (production data)
examples.code:
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db \
  --mount source=pgdata,target=/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:15

examples.label: Bind mount (development)
examples.code:
docker run -d --name dev \
  --mount type=bind,source="$(pwd)"/src,target=/app/src \
  node:20-alpine npm run dev   # edit src on the host, app reloads

examples.label: tmpfs (in-memory, ephemeral)
examples.code:
docker run -d --name cache \
  --mount type=tmpfs,target=/scratch,tmpfs-size=64m \
  myapp

tips: Use named volumes for persistent data, bind mounts for live dev code, tmpfs for secrets/scratch.
Prefer the explicit --mount syntax over -v; it's clearer and fails loudly on typos.
Keep database data on a named volume so upgrades and container recreation don't lose it.
gotchas: -v auto-creates a host directory if the source path doesn't exist, silently giving you an empty bind mount (a classic confusion).
Bind-mounting over an image directory hides whatever the image shipped there.
tmpfs data lives in RAM and disappears on stop — great for secrets, terrible for anything you need to keep.

lessons.theory: Named volumes have their own lifecycle, independent of containers. You create them (explicitly with docker volume create or implicitly when first mounted), they persist after the container that used them is removed, and you must delete them deliberately. This independence is a feature — your database survives a container recreation — but it also means volumes accumulate. docker volume ls lists them, docker volume inspect shows the mountpoint and driver, docker volume rm deletes one, and docker volume prune removes all volumes not currently used by any container. Be careful: prune is irreversible and a stray prune can wipe a database. Notably, docker rm by default does NOT remove the container's named volumes (you need -v, and even that only removes anonymous volumes).

examples.label: List, inspect, remove
examples.code:
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect pgdata
docker volume rm pgdata          # only when unused

examples.label: Prune unused volumes (dangerous)
examples.code:
docker volume prune              # removes ALL volumes not attached to a container
docker volume prune --filter label!=keep   # spare labelled ones

examples.label: Anonymous volumes pile up
examples.code:
docker run -d -v /var/lib/mysql mysql:8   # creates an anonymous volume each run
docker volume ls   # see the random-hash volumes accumulate

tips: Name your volumes meaningfully so you never confuse a prod database volume with scratch.
Label important volumes and exclude them from prune with a filter.
Audit volumes periodically with docker volume ls; anonymous volumes from -v without a name accumulate silently.
gotchas: docker volume prune is irreversible — one careless run can destroy a database that wasn't attached at that moment.
Anonymous volumes (from -v /path with no name) multiply on every run and are hard to track.
Removing a container does not remove its named volumes — good for safety, but they linger until you clean up.

lessons.theory: A single named volume can be mounted into multiple containers simultaneously, which is how you share data between them — for example, a web app writing uploads that a worker processes, or one container generating files another serves. Mount the same volume by name in each container. The older --volumes-from flag attaches all of another container's volumes, useful for sidecar/backup patterns. Sharing requires coordination: concurrent writers to the same files can corrupt data unless the application handles locking, so the safe patterns are one writer / many readers, or partitioned writes. For network/cluster scenarios where containers run on different hosts, a local named volume isn't shared across hosts — you need a networked volume driver (NFS, cloud) covered later.

examples.label: Two containers share one volume
examples.code:
docker volume create shared
docker run -d --name writer --mount source=shared,target=/data writer-img
docker run -d --name reader --mount source=shared,target=/data reader-img

examples.label: Sidecar via --volumes-from
examples.code:
docker run -d --name app -v appdata:/data myapp
docker run --rm --volumes-from app alpine ls /data   # backup/inspect sidecar

examples.label: Read-only mount for safety
examples.code:
docker run -d --name reader \
  --mount source=shared,target=/data,readonly reader-img

tips: Mount shared data read-only (,readonly) in consumers to prevent accidental writes and corruption.
Prefer one-writer/many-reader designs; coordinate if multiple writers are unavoidable.
Use --volumes-from for short-lived backup/inspection sidecars.
gotchas: Multiple writers to the same files without locking can corrupt data — Docker doesn't arbitrate access.
A local named volume is single-host; containers on different machines won't see each other's writes without a network driver.
Sharing a database's data directory between two database containers will corrupt it — databases expect exclusive access.

lessons.theory: Because volume data lives outside containers, backups are done by running a throwaway container that mounts the volume plus a host directory and copies between them — typically tar'ing the volume's contents to a file on the host, and untar'ing to restore. This pattern works for any volume regardless of its driver. For databases, prefer the database's own dump tools (pg_dump, mysqldump) over raw file copies when the database is running, because copying live data files can capture an inconsistent state; stop the container or use the DB's consistent-snapshot mechanism. Automate backups on a schedule, store them off-host (object storage), and — critically — test restores regularly, because an untested backup is just a hope.

examples.label: Back up a volume to a tarball
examples.code:
docker run --rm \
  -v pgdata:/data:ro \
  -v "$(pwd)":/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /data .

examples.label: Restore from a tarball
examples.code:
docker run --rm \
  -v pgdata:/data \
  -v "$(pwd)":/backup \
  alpine sh -c 'cd /data && tar xzf /backup/pgdata-2026-06-19.tar.gz'

examples.label: Consistent DB dump (preferred for live DBs)
examples.code: docker exec db pg_dump -U user mydb > mydb-$(date +%F).sql

tips: For live databases use native dump tools (pg_dump/mysqldump) instead of copying raw data files.
Schedule backups, push them off-host, and rotate retention — and actually test a restore.
Mount the source volume read-only (:ro) during backup so the job can't mutate it.
gotchas: Copying a running database's files can capture a torn, unrestorable state — stop it or use a proper dump.
A backup you've never restored is unverified — schedule restore drills.
Backups stored on the same host die with the host; keep copies elsewhere.

lessons.theory: Moving volume data between hosts, drivers, or environments comes up during upgrades, host replacement, and cloud migrations. The portable approach mirrors backup/restore: tar the source volume, transfer the archive (scp/rsync/object storage), and untar into a fresh volume on the destination. For host-to-host you can even stream directly over SSH without an intermediate file. When changing a database's major version, a raw volume copy often won't work because on-disk formats change — use the database's dump/restore so the data is re-imported in the new format. Plan migrations with a maintenance window or a replication/dual-write strategy for zero-downtime, and always keep the source intact until the destination is verified.

examples.label: Stream a volume to another host over SSH
examples.code:
docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data:ro alpine tar czf - -C /data . \
  | ssh user@newhost 'docker run --rm -i -v pgdata:/data alpine tar xzf - -C /data'

examples.label: Major-version DB upgrade via dump
examples.code:
docker exec old-db pg_dumpall -U postgres > all.sql
# start new major version, then:
cat all.sql | docker exec -i new-db psql -U postgres

examples.label: Verify before deleting the source
examples.code: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data:ro alpine sh -c 'ls -la /data && du -sh /data'

tips: Keep the source volume untouched until you've validated the destination.
For database major upgrades, migrate via dump/restore, not raw file copy.
Stream over SSH for host-to-host moves to skip a large intermediate file.
gotchas: Raw-copying database files across major versions usually fails — incompatible on-disk formats.
UID/GID ownership can change across hosts; fix permissions on the destination so the app can read its data.
Forgetting to stop writers during migration leads to lost writes between snapshot and cutover.

lessons.theory: The default local volume driver stores data on a single host. To share a volume across multiple hosts or to back it with managed storage, you use volume drivers and plugins. A volume can be backed by NFS (so several Docker hosts mount the same network share), or by cloud block/file storage via plugins (AWS EBS/EFS, Azure Files, GCP Persistent Disk). In orchestration this is generalised: Docker Swarm uses driver options, and Kubernetes formalises it as the CSI (Container Storage Interface) with PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses that dynamically provision cloud disks. Networked storage trades some latency for shared, durable, and often replicated data — essential when a container can be rescheduled onto a different node and must find its data there.

examples.label: Create an NFS-backed volume
examples.code:
docker volume create --driver local \
  --opt type=nfs \
  --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw,nfsvers=4 \
  --opt device=:/exports/appdata appdata
docker run -d -v appdata:/data myapp

examples.label: Use a cloud plugin (conceptual)
examples.code:
docker plugin install rexray/ebs   # cloud block-storage plugin
docker volume create -d rexray/ebs --opt size=20 ebsdata

examples.label: Kubernetes CSI equivalent (where this leads)
examples.code:
# PersistentVolumeClaim -> StorageClass -> CSI driver provisions a cloud disk
kubectl get storageclass

tips: Use NFS or a cloud driver when containers must share data or be rescheduled across hosts.
Match the storage type to the workload: block (EBS) for databases, file (EFS/NFS) for shared content.
In Kubernetes, this becomes CSI + PersistentVolumes — the same idea with dynamic provisioning.
gotchas: Network storage adds latency and a network dependency — a flaky NFS server can stall every container using it.
Many cloud block volumes (EBS) attach to one node at a time — they don't support multi-host read-write like a file share does.
Driver/plugin version mismatches and auth misconfig are common failure points; test failover before relying on it.

lessons.theory: Docker Compose describes a multi-container application declaratively in a single YAML file (compose.yaml, formerly docker-compose.yml). Instead of long docker run commands, you define services (containers), and optionally networks and volumes, then bring the whole stack up with docker compose up. The modern Compose Specification dropped the top-level version: key — it's no longer needed. The core top-level keys are services (each a named container with its image/build, ports, environment, volumes, etc.), networks, and volumes. Compose v2 is a Docker CLI plugin invoked as docker compose (space, not hyphen). The value is reproducibility and convenience: the file is version-controlled, self-documents the architecture, and lets anyone start the entire app with one command.

examples.label: A minimal modern compose.yaml
examples.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:

examples.label: Core lifecycle commands
examples.code:
docker compose up -d        # start the stack detached
docker compose ps           # what's running
docker compose logs -f web  # tail a service
docker compose down         # stop and remove (add -v to drop volumes)

examples.label: Validate and view the merged config
examples.code: docker compose config       # prints the fully-resolved configuration

tips: Omit the obsolete top-level 'version:' key — the Compose Spec doesn't need it.
Use 'docker compose config' to validate syntax and see the final resolved file.
Keep compose.yaml in version control as living documentation of your stack.
gotchas: It's 'docker compose' (v2 plugin), not the old 'docker-compose' binary — behaviour and flags differ slightly.
YAML is indentation-sensitive; a stray tab or wrong indent produces confusing parse errors.
docker compose down -v deletes named volumes too — easy to wipe data by adding -v out of habit.

lessons.theory: A service is the Compose unit: a container definition that can either build from a local Dockerfile (build:) or use a prebuilt image (image:), plus its ports, environment, volumes, command, and restart policy. By default Compose creates one network for the project and attaches every service to it, so services reach each other by service name via DNS — no manual networking needed. You can define additional named networks to segment tiers (e.g. a backend network the database sits on, isolated from a frontend network). Named volumes declared under the top-level volumes: key persist data across up/down cycles. This trio — services, networks, volumes — maps directly to the docker run, docker network, and docker volume concepts you already know, just declared instead of imperative.

examples.label: Segment tiers with custom networks
examples.code:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    networks: [frontend]
  api:
    build: ./api
    networks: [frontend, backend]
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    networks: [backend]      # unreachable from 'web'
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]

networks:
  frontend:
  backend:
volumes:
  pgdata:

examples.label: build vs image
examples.code:
services:
  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.prod
      args:
        NODE_VERSION: "20"
  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine

examples.label: Restart policy
examples.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    restart: unless-stopped

tips: Let Compose's default network handle service-to-service DNS; add custom networks only to isolate tiers.
Declare databases on a backend-only network so the public service can't reach them directly.
Use restart: unless-stopped for long-running services so they survive daemon restarts.
gotchas: Volumes defined inline but not under the top-level volumes: key may become anonymous and not persist as you expect.
A service on only the backend network can't be reached by one on only the frontend network — by design, but a common surprise.
build: rebuilds only when you ask (--build or up --build); a stale image can hide your latest code.

lessons.theory: Compose has two distinct env mechanisms that are easy to conflate. The first is variable substitution in the YAML itself: ${VAR} placeholders in compose.yaml are filled from your shell environment or from a .env file sitting next to the compose file — this parameterises the file (image tags, ports). The second is container environment: the environment: key (or env_file:) sets variables inside the running service. So .env (auto-loaded, for substitution) is different from env_file: (explicitly listed files whose contents become container env vars). Keep real secrets out of both committed files — use a local untracked .env or, better, Docker/orchestrator secrets. Use environment: with ${VAR} substitution to pass a value from your shell through into the container without hardcoding it.

examples.label: Substitution from a .env file
examples.code:
# .env (next to compose.yaml, auto-loaded)
POSTGRES_VERSION=15
APP_PORT=8080

# compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:${POSTGRES_VERSION}
  web:
    ports:
      - "${APP_PORT}:80"

examples.label: Container env via env_file and environment
examples.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    env_file:
      - ./api.env          # contents become env vars INSIDE the container
    environment:
      LOG_LEVEL: info
      DB_HOST: db

examples.label: Pass a shell secret through without hardcoding
examples.code:
# environment value comes from your shell at 'up' time
services:
  api:
    environment:
      API_TOKEN: ${API_TOKEN}
# run: API_TOKEN=xyz docker compose up -d

tips: Remember: .env feeds ${VAR} substitution in the YAML; env_file: sets variables inside the container — different jobs.
Gitignore your .env and commit a .env.example template instead.
Use ${VAR:-default} to provide fallbacks for optional substitution variables.
gotchas: Committing a .env with real credentials leaks secrets — keep it untracked.
Confusing .env (substitution) with env_file: (container vars) leads to variables that 'don't show up' where expected.
An unset substitution variable expands to an empty string and can silently produce 'image:' or 'port ::80' errors.

lessons.theory: depends_on controls start order, but plain depends_on only waits for the dependency container to START, not to be READY — Postgres's process can be up while the database is still initialising and refusing connections. The robust pattern combines a healthcheck on the dependency with depends_on: condition: service_healthy, so Compose waits until the dependency reports healthy before starting the dependent service. A healthcheck is a command Docker runs periodically (test:) with an interval, timeout, and retries; the container's status becomes healthy or unhealthy. Even with this, well-built apps should still retry their connections at runtime, because dependencies can restart at any time. depends_on does not work across separate compose files or across machines — it's a single-stack, start-order tool.

examples.label: Wait for the database to be truly ready
examples.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
  api:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

examples.label: App-level healthcheck
examples.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-qO-", "http://localhost:3000/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
