      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s

examples.label: Check health status
examples.code:
docker compose ps   # shows (healthy)/(unhealthy)
docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <container>

tips: Pair depends_on with condition: service_healthy + a real healthcheck — start order alone isn't readiness.
Set start_period to give slow-booting services grace before failures count.
Still implement connection retries in the app; dependencies can restart after startup.
gotchas: Plain depends_on only waits for 'started', not 'ready' — the classic 'connection refused on first boot' bug.
A healthcheck that always passes (or a missing one) defeats condition: service_healthy.
depends_on is ignored across separate compose projects/files — it's not a cross-stack coordinator.

lessons.theory: Compose can run multiple replicas of a stateless service with docker compose up --scale service=N (or the deploy.replicas key). Compose's built-in network load-balances connections to the service name across the replicas via DNS round-robin, so other services keep using the same hostname. Two constraints follow: you cannot statically publish a fixed host port for a scaled service (three replicas can't all bind host:8080) — let Docker assign ports or front them with a reverse proxy/load balancer; and only stateless services scale cleanly, because replicas don't share local state. Compose scaling is great for local testing of horizontal behaviour, but real production horizontal scaling, rolling updates, and self-healing belong to an orchestrator (Swarm or Kubernetes).

examples.label: Scale a stateless worker
examples.code:
docker compose up -d --scale worker=4
docker compose ps   # four worker replicas

examples.label: deploy.replicas in the file
examples.code:
services:
  worker:
    build: ./worker
    deploy:
      replicas: 3

examples.label: Front replicas with a proxy (no fixed host port)
examples.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    # no fixed 'ports:' — scaled
  proxy:
    image: nginx
    ports: ["8080:80"]
    depends_on: [api]   # nginx upstreams to api (DNS round-robins replicas)

tips: Only scale stateless services; keep state in shared databases/volumes, not in the replicas.
Don't pin a host port on a scaled service — use a reverse proxy or let Docker assign ports.
Use scaling locally to validate horizontal behaviour before moving to an orchestrator.
gotchas: Scaling a service with a fixed 'ports: 8080:80' fails — replicas collide on the host port.
Stateful services (a single database) don't scale by replication this way — you'll corrupt or fork state.
Compose scaling has no rolling updates or self-healing — that's orchestrator territory.

lessons.theory: Profiles let one compose file carry optional services that only start when their profile is activated, avoiding the proliferation of near-duplicate files. You tag a service with profiles: [debug] (or [dev], [tools]) and it stays dormant during a normal docker compose up; it starts only when you pass --profile debug or set COMPOSE_PROFILES. This is ideal for optional helpers — a database admin UI, a seed/migration runner, a mailcatcher — that you want in development but not production. Services without any profile always run. Combined with override files and environment variables, profiles give you a single source of truth that adapts to dev, test, and prod without copy-paste drift.

examples.label: Tag optional services with profiles
examples.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .            # no profile -> always runs
  adminer:
    image: adminer
    profiles: ["dev"]   # only with the 'dev' profile
  seed:
    build: ./seed
    profiles: ["tools"]

examples.label: Activate a profile
examples.code:
docker compose --profile dev up -d        # starts app + adminer
COMPOSE_PROFILES=dev,tools docker compose up -d

examples.label: Default run skips profiled services
examples.code: docker compose up -d   # starts only 'app' (adminer/seed stay dormant)

tips: Use profiles for optional dev-only helpers (admin UIs, seeders) so prod runs stay lean.
Set COMPOSE_PROFILES in your shell/CI to activate the right set per environment.
Services with no profile always start — keep your core stack profile-free.
gotchas: A profiled service won't start on a plain 'up' — forgetting --profile makes it look 'missing'.
A service depending on a profiled service can fail if that dependency's profile isn't active.
Profiles control whether a service starts, not configuration differences — combine with overrides for that.

lessons.theory: Compose automatically merges compose.yaml with compose.override.yaml when both exist, layering the override on top of the base. This is the idiomatic way to keep a shared base definition while customising per environment: the base holds what's common, and the override adds dev-only things like bind-mounting source for live reload, exposing debug ports, or relaxing settings. For production you typically don't use the auto-loaded override; instead you pass explicit files with -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml so only the intended layers apply. Merge rules: scalars are replaced, lists are generally appended, and maps are merged — so an override can add a volume or env var without restating the whole service.

examples.label: Base + auto-loaded dev override
examples.code:
# compose.yaml (base)
services:
  app:
    image: myapp:latest
    ports: ["8080:80"]

# compose.override.yaml (auto-merged for dev)
services:
  app:
    build: .                 # build locally instead of pulling
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src       # live-reload source
    environment:
      DEBUG: "true"

examples.label: Explicit prod composition (no auto-override)
examples.code: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d

examples.label: See the merged result
examples.code: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml config

tips: Keep environment-agnostic config in the base and environment-specific bits in overrides.
For prod, compose explicitly with -f files so the dev override isn't silently applied.
Run 'compose config' on your -f combination to confirm exactly what will run.
gotchas: compose.override.yaml is auto-loaded — it can apply dev settings in places you didn't intend if you forget it exists.
List vs map merge behaviour differs (lists append, maps merge); unexpected duplicates can appear.
Order matters with multiple -f files: later files override earlier ones.

lessons.theory: Compose is handy in CI for spinning up an app together with its real dependencies (database, cache, message broker) to run integration and end-to-end tests in an environment that mirrors production. A typical job brings the stack up, waits for healthchecks, runs the test suite against it, captures logs, and tears everything down. Use docker compose up -d with healthchecks so tests start only when dependencies are ready, run tests in a dedicated service or via docker compose run, and always docker compose down -v at the end to clean state. For deployment, Compose suits single-host targets (a VM running docker compose up with a pinned image tag); multi-node deployments are better handled by an orchestrator. Pin image tags by digest or SHA in CI so the tested artifact is exactly what deploys.

examples.label: Integration test stack in CI
examples.code:
docker compose -f compose.ci.yaml up -d --wait   # --wait blocks until healthy
docker compose -f compose.ci.yaml run --rm tests pytest
docker compose -f compose.ci.yaml logs --no-color > logs.txt
docker compose -f compose.ci.yaml down -v

examples.label: GitHub Actions step
examples.code:
- name: Integration tests
  run: |
    docker compose up -d --wait
    docker compose run --rm tests npm run test:integration
    docker compose down -v

examples.label: Deploy to a single host
examples.code:
ssh deploy@host 'cd /srv/app && \
  docker compose pull && docker compose up -d'

tips: Use 'docker compose up --wait' so the job blocks until all healthchecks pass before testing.
Always 'down -v' at the end of CI jobs to avoid leaking state between runs.
Pin image tags (digest/SHA) in CI so the tested image is exactly what you deploy.
gotchas: Without healthchecks, tests start before the database is ready and fail intermittently (flaky CI).
Forgetting down -v leaves volumes/networks that pollute the next run on a shared runner.
Compose is single-host; don't try to use it as a multi-node production orchestrator.

lessons.theory: By default a container's processes run as root (UID 0), and because the container shares the host kernel, container-root is close to host-root if isolation is ever broken. Running as a non-root user is the single highest-impact hardening step. In the Dockerfile, create a dedicated user and switch to it with USER before the CMD/ENTRYPOINT, so the application runs unprivileged. Many official images already provide a non-root user (e.g. node ships a node user). Use a numeric UID where possible so Kubernetes runAsNonRoot can enforce it and so the identity is unambiguous. You must ensure the non-root user owns the files and directories it needs (chown during build), or the app will hit permission errors at runtime.

examples.label: Create and switch to a non-root user (Debian)
examples.code:
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app -u 1001 app \
 && chown -R app:app /app
USER 1001
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

examples.label: Alpine equivalent
examples.code:
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S -G app -u 1001 app
USER app

examples.label: Enforce at runtime
examples.code:
docker run --user 1001 myapp
# Kubernetes: securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1001

tips: Add USER (a numeric UID) before CMD so the app never runs as root.
chown the app's files to the runtime user during build to avoid permission errors.
Prefer official images' built-in non-root users (e.g. 'node') when available.
gotchas: Switching USER without fixing file ownership causes 'permission denied' at startup.
A non-root user usually can't bind ports below 1024 — listen on 8080 not 80, or grant the capability explicitly.
Some images reset to root in later layers; verify the FINAL USER is non-root with docker inspect.

lessons.theory: A compromised process that can write to the container filesystem can drop tools, modify binaries, or persist. Running the container with a read-only root filesystem (--read-only) removes that capability: the union filesystem is mounted read-only, so the app can't write anywhere it shouldn't. Real apps still need some writable space (temp files, caches, PID files), which you provide narrowly with tmpfs mounts or specific writable volumes for just those paths. This least-privilege posture — read-only root plus a couple of explicitly writable, often in-memory, directories — dramatically limits what an attacker can do post-exploitation and is a recommended default for production workloads, mirrored by Kubernetes' readOnlyRootFilesystem securityContext.

examples.label: Read-only root + writable tmp
examples.code:
docker run --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m \
  --tmpfs /run:rw \
  myapp

examples.label: Compose form
examples.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
    volumes:
      - cache:/var/cache/app   # only this path is writable+persistent

examples.label: Kubernetes equivalent
examples.code:
# securityContext:
#   readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
# plus an emptyDir volume mounted at /tmp

tips: Default to --read-only in production and open only the specific paths the app must write.
Use tmpfs for writable scratch/temp so nothing persists and writes stay in RAM.
Audit which directories your app writes (strace/logs) so you mount exactly those.
gotchas: Many apps write to /tmp, /run, or a cache dir — read-only without those tmpfs mounts crashes them.
Logging to a file inside the container breaks under read-only; log to stdout instead.
Frameworks that compile templates/assets at runtime need a writable path or a build-time pre-compile.

lessons.theory: Linux splits root's powers into ~40 discrete capabilities (CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, CAP_CHOWN, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, etc.). Docker already drops many by default, but most containers still hold more than they need. The hardening pattern is to drop ALL capabilities and then add back only the few the app genuinely requires — for example CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE if it must bind a low port. This shrinks the blast radius: even running as root with no capabilities, a process can't perform privileged operations like raw socket access, mounting filesystems, or changing file ownership. The most dangerous setting is the opposite, --privileged, which grants essentially all capabilities and device access and effectively dissolves the container boundary; it should be avoided outside very specific tooling.

examples.label: Drop all, add back only what's needed
examples.code:
docker run \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  myapp   # can bind :80 but nothing else privileged

examples.label: Compose form
examples.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    cap_add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true

examples.label: Avoid --privileged
examples.code:
# DON'T: docker run --privileged ...  (grants almost everything)
# Prefer specific --cap-add or --device for the exact need

tips: Drop ALL capabilities, then add back the minimum (often just NET_BIND_SERVICE or none).
Add --security-opt no-new-privileges:true to block privilege escalation via setuid binaries.
Use --device to grant a specific device instead of --privileged.
gotchas: --privileged disables most isolation (all caps + device access) — almost never appropriate for app containers.
Dropping a capability the app actually needs causes obscure failures (e.g. can't bind port, can't chown).
Capabilities are separate from the user: even non-root can be over-privileged if you don't drop caps.

lessons.theory: Beyond capabilities, two kernel mechanisms restrict what a container can do at the syscall and resource level. Seccomp (secure computing mode) filters which system calls a process may make; Docker applies a default seccomp profile that already blocks dozens of dangerous syscalls, and you can supply a tighter custom profile for high-security workloads. AppArmor (on Debian/Ubuntu) and SELinux (on RHEL/Fedora) are Mandatory Access Control systems that confine a container to an allowed set of file paths, capabilities, and operations via a policy profile; Docker ships a default AppArmor profile too. Together with non-root, read-only root, and dropped capabilities, these form defence-in-depth: each layer assumes the others might fail. For most teams the defaults are a solid baseline; custom profiles are for hardening sensitive services.

examples.label: Apply a custom seccomp profile
examples.code:
docker run --security-opt seccomp=./tight-seccomp.json myapp
# Don't disable it: --security-opt seccomp=unconfined removes the protection

examples.label: Apply an AppArmor profile
examples.code:
docker run --security-opt apparmor=docker-default myapp
# or a custom loaded profile: apparmor=my-app-profile

examples.label: Compose security_opt
examples.code:
services:
  app:
    security_opt:
      - seccomp=./tight-seccomp.json
      - no-new-privileges:true

tips: Keep the default seccomp and AppArmor/SELinux profiles enabled — they block real attack syscalls for free.
Write a custom seccomp profile only for hardened, sensitive services after profiling their syscalls.
Combine with non-root + dropped caps + read-only root for layered defence.
gotchas: --security-opt seccomp=unconfined disables syscall filtering entirely — a big, easy-to-miss regression.
Overly tight custom profiles break apps with cryptic 'operation not permitted' errors; test thoroughly.
AppArmor vs SELinux depends on the host distro — a profile from one doesn't apply to the other.

lessons.theory: Images inherit vulnerabilities from their base OS packages and application dependencies. Image scanners inspect an image's package inventory and dependency manifests, compare them against CVE databases, and report known vulnerabilities by severity, often with the fixed version. Trivy (open-source, fast, widely used) and Snyk are common choices; Docker Scout is built in. Scanning belongs in two places: locally/pre-commit for fast feedback, and in CI as a gate that fails the build when high/critical, fixable CVEs are found. Scanning is necessary but not sufficient — also keep base images current, rebuild regularly so patched packages flow in, and pin by digest so you scan exactly what ships. A clean scan today can have new CVEs tomorrow, so rescan on a schedule.

examples.label: Scan an image with Trivy
examples.code:
trivy image myapp:latest
# Fail CI only on fixable high/critical issues:
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 myapp:latest

examples.label: Scan in GitHub Actions
examples.code:
- uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
    severity: HIGH,CRITICAL
    exit-code: '1'
    ignore-unfixed: true

examples.label: Docker Scout (built in)
examples.code: docker scout cves myapp:latest

tips: Gate CI on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs (--ignore-unfixed) so you act only on actionable findings.
Rebuild images regularly so base-image security patches actually reach production.
Scan the exact digest you deploy, and rescan on a schedule — new CVEs appear constantly.
gotchas: A passing scan is point-in-time; an unchanged image accrues new CVEs over weeks.
Failing on unfixable CVEs creates noise and alert fatigue — filter to fixable ones.
Scanners catch known CVEs only — they don't find your own logic flaws or misconfigurations.

lessons.theory: Secrets — passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates — must never be baked into images or passed via build ARG/ENV. ARG values persist in image build history; ENV values are visible in docker inspect, in process listings, and to every process in the container, and they leak into logs and crash dumps. The correct approaches: at build time, use BuildKit secret mounts (RUN --mount=type=secret) so the value is available to one command and never written to a layer; at run time, inject secrets through Docker/Swarm secrets (mounted as files under /run/secrets), Kubernetes Secrets, or an external secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, cloud KMS). Mounting secrets as files is safer than env vars because files aren't exposed by inspect and can be access-controlled. Rotate secrets and keep them out of version control entirely.

examples.label: Build-time secret (never in a layer)
examples.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmtoken \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npmtoken) npm ci
# docker build --secret id=npmtoken,src=$HOME/.npmtoken .

examples.label: Runtime secret as a mounted file (Compose)
examples.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    secrets: [db_password]
    environment:
      DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password   # app reads the file
secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./db_password.txt   # untracked

examples.label: External manager (conceptual)
examples.code:
# App fetches at startup from Vault / AWS Secrets Manager via IAM,
# so nothing sensitive lives in the image or compose file.

tips: Inject secrets as mounted files (/run/secrets/...) rather than env vars — they won't show in docker inspect.
Use BuildKit --secret for any build-time credential; never ARG/ENV a secret.
Centralise with Vault or a cloud secrets manager and rotate regularly.
gotchas: ENV secrets are visible via docker inspect, /proc, and crash logs — treat any ENV secret as already leaked.
ARG secrets are permanently recorded in image history even if 'removed' later.
Committing a secrets file (or .env) to git exposes it forever in history — rotate immediately if it happens.

lessons.theory: Container networking is part of the security boundary. Principles: don't publish ports you don't need (every -p is exposed surface); bind administrative and database ports to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0 so they aren't reachable from the LAN; segment the application into network tiers so the public edge can't reach the data tier directly; and put internal-only services on networks with no host port publishing at all. For stricter setups, use internal networks (no external connectivity) for backends, and a reverse proxy as the single controlled ingress. The goal is least privilege at the network layer: a compromised frontend should not have a direct path to the database, and nothing internal should be reachable from outside without passing a controlled gateway.

examples.label: Internal backend network (no host access)
examples.code:
services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx
    ports: ["443:443"]      # the only public ingress
    networks: [edge, app]
  api:
    build: .
    networks: [app, data]
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    networks: [data]         # no ports: published
networks:
  edge:
  app:
  data:
    internal: true           # no external connectivity at all

examples.label: Bind a DB to localhost only
examples.code: docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 postgres:15

examples.label: Don't publish internal services
examples.code:
# A cache used only by the API needs NO 'ports:' entry —
# the API reaches it by service name on the shared network.

tips: Publish only what truly needs external access; bind admin/db ports to 127.0.0.1.
Segment tiers (edge/app/data) and mark backend networks 'internal: true'.
Use a single reverse proxy as controlled ingress instead of exposing each service.
gotchas: -p defaults to 0.0.0.0, exposing services to the whole network — explicitly bind to localhost for private ones.
Putting the database on the same flat network as the public service gives attackers a direct path to data.
An 'internal: true' network has no internet access — services needing outbound calls must sit on a non-internal network too.

lessons.theory: Docker Bench for Security is an automated script that checks a Docker host and its containers against the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Docker Benchmark — dozens of best-practice controls covering host configuration, the daemon, daemon files and permissions, container runtime settings, and image build hygiene. Running it produces a pass/warn/info report that highlights misconfigurations like an exposed daemon socket, containers running privileged, missing user namespaces, or world-writable files. It's a fast way to baseline a host's posture and to catch regressions over time. Treat it as a checklist and prioritisation tool rather than a guarantee: fix the high-severity warnings, document accepted risks, and re-run it as part of host provisioning and periodic audits.

examples.label: Run Docker Bench against the host
examples.code:
docker run --rm --net host --pid host --userns host --cap-add audit_control \
  -v /var/lib:/var/lib:ro \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro \
  -v /etc:/etc:ro \
  docker/docker-bench-security

examples.label: Focus on a section
examples.code:
# The script groups checks: 1 Host, 2 Daemon, 4 Container Images,
# 5 Container Runtime — start by clearing [WARN] in 5 (runtime).

examples.label: Re-run as a periodic audit
examples.code: # Schedule it (cron/CI) so posture regressions are caught early.

tips: Run Docker Bench on new hosts to baseline against the CIS benchmark, then fix [WARN] items.
Prioritise runtime (section 5) findings — they map to live container risk.
Re-run periodically; configuration drifts and new containers reintroduce issues.
gotchas: Bench reflects CIS best practice, not your threat model — some warnings are acceptable in context (document them).
It needs broad host mounts/permissions to inspect everything — run it deliberately, not as a routine privileged container.
A clean bench report doesn't cover app-level vulnerabilities or image CVEs — pair it with scanning.

lessons.theory: A registry stores and distributes images; Docker Hub is the default public registry. An image reference is registry/namespace/repository:tag — when you omit the registry, Docker assumes docker.io (Hub), which is why docker pull nginx works. To publish, you log in (docker login), tag your image with your namespace (yourname/app:1.0), and docker push it; others docker pull it back. Tags are mutable pointers, so for reproducibility consumers should pin by immutable digest (@sha256:...). Be aware of Hub's rate limits on anonymous and free pulls, which can break CI that pulls heavily — authenticate or mirror to avoid throttling. Public repos are world-readable; private repos require auth.

examples.label: Tag, log in, push
examples.code:
docker login
docker tag myapp:1.0 eknatha/myapp:1.0
docker push eknatha/myapp:1.0

examples.label: Pull (registry defaults to Docker Hub)
examples.code:
docker pull eknatha/myapp:1.0     # = docker.io/eknatha/myapp:1.0
docker pull nginx                  # = docker.io/library/nginx:latest

examples.label: Pin by digest for reproducibility
examples.code: docker pull nginx@sha256:abc123...   # exact bytes, tag-proof

tips: Authenticate in CI even for public pulls to avoid Hub's anonymous rate limits.
Pin production images by @sha256 digest so a re-pushed tag can't change what you run.
Use a clear tagging scheme (semver + git SHA) rather than relying on :latest.
gotchas: Anonymous/free Hub pull rate limits can intermittently break CI — a surprisingly common outage cause.
Pushing without your namespace prefix fails (you can't push to library/...).
Tags are mutable: someone re-pushing your:tag changes it underneath consumers who didn't pin a digest.

lessons.theory: GHCR (ghcr.io) is GitHub's image registry, tightly integrated with GitHub repos and Actions. Images live under ghcr.io/OWNER/IMAGE and can be linked to a repository, inheriting visibility and access controls. In GitHub Actions you authenticate using the automatically-provided GITHUB_TOKEN (no separate secret needed for same-repo pushes), which makes build-and-push pipelines simple and secure. GHCR supports fine-grained permissions, package visibility (public/private), and retention policies for cleaning old versions. It's a natural choice when your source already lives on GitHub: one place for code, CI, and images, with tokens scoped to the repo rather than long-lived credentials.

examples.label: Push to GHCR from Actions
Manual login with a PAT
examples.code:
echo $CR_PAT | docker login ghcr.io -u eknatha --password-stdin
docker push ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp:1.0

examples.label: Grant the workflow package permission
examples.code:
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write   # required for GITHUB_TOKEN to push to GHCR

tips: Use the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN for same-repo pushes — no long-lived secret to manage.
Add 'permissions: packages: write' to the workflow or the push will be denied.
Set package visibility and retention policies to keep the registry tidy.
gotchas: Forgetting 'packages: write' permission causes a 403 on push even with a valid token.
New GHCR packages default to private; consumers get 'denied' until visibility or access is granted.
A personal access token for GHCR needs the right scopes (write:packages) — a generic token won't work.

lessons.theory: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) is AWS's managed private registry, commonly paired with ECS, EKS, and Lambda. Authentication is short-lived and IAM-based: you call aws ecr get-login-password to obtain a temporary token and pipe it into docker login. Each repository has a URI like ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/REPO. You create repositories explicitly (or via IaC), and ECR offers image scanning, lifecycle policies to expire old images, and cross-account/region replication. In CI you authenticate using an IAM role (OIDC from GitHub Actions, or an instance role) rather than static keys. The key mental difference from Hub is that ECR auth tokens expire (~12 hours), so you re-authenticate as part of each pipeline run rather than storing a permanent password.

examples.label: Authenticate and push to ECR
examples.code:
aws ecr get-login-password --region ap-south-1 \
  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin \
    123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com

docker tag myapp:1.0 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:1.0
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:1.0

examples.label: Create a repo and set a lifecycle policy
examples.code:
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name myapp
# Lifecycle policy: expire untagged images older than 14 days

examples.label: CI auth via OIDC role (no static keys)
examples.code:
- uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
  with:
    role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/gha-ecr-push
    aws-region: ap-south-1
- uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2

tips: Use IAM roles + OIDC in CI instead of long-lived AWS access keys.
Add ECR lifecycle policies to auto-expire old/untagged images and control storage cost.
Enable ECR scan-on-push for built-in vulnerability detection.
gotchas: ECR login tokens expire (~12h) — you must re-authenticate each pipeline run, not store a password.
The repository must exist before you push; ECR won't auto-create it like some registries.
The full registry URI (account.dkr.ecr.region...) is required in the tag — a short name won't resolve.

lessons.theory: You can self-host a registry using the open-source registry:2 image (the Distribution project). It's a simple HTTP service that stores images on a filesystem or object-storage backend. Running your own is useful for air-gapped environments, full control, or avoiding third-party limits, but it shifts operational burden to you: you must add TLS (the registry should not run plaintext in production), authentication (an htpasswd file or a token service), storage management, and garbage collection to reclaim space from deleted images. For richer needs (UI, RBAC, scanning, replication, signing) teams often run Harbor, which wraps Distribution with enterprise features. The core trade-off: self-hosting maximises control and isolation at the cost of running and securing the infrastructure yourself.

examples.label: Run a local registry (dev only)
examples.code:
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry registry:2
docker tag myapp:1.0 localhost:5000/myapp:1.0
docker push localhost:5000/myapp:1.0

examples.label: Add basic auth + TLS (production-ish)
examples.code:
docker run -d -p 443:5000 --name registry \
  -v $(pwd)/certs:/certs -v $(pwd)/auth:/auth \
  -e REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_CERTIFICATE=/certs/domain.crt \
  -e REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_KEY=/certs/domain.key \
  -e REGISTRY_AUTH=htpasswd \
  -e REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_PATH=/auth/htpasswd \
  -e REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_REALM='Registry' \
  registry:2

examples.label: Reclaim space via garbage collection
examples.code: docker exec registry registry garbage-collect /etc/docker/registry/config.yml

tips: Always add TLS and authentication before any non-local use of a self-hosted registry.
Consider Harbor when you need a UI, RBAC, scanning, replication, or signing out of the box.
Schedule garbage collection; deleting image tags alone doesn't free the underlying blobs.
gotchas: An insecure (plaintext) registry requires special daemon config and is unsafe outside localhost.
Deleting tags doesn't reclaim disk — you must run garbage-collect to free blobs.
Self-hosting means you own backups, TLS renewal, and uptime — non-trivial operational work.

lessons.theory: Pulling an image by tag tells you nothing about who built it or whether it was tampered with. Image signing closes that supply-chain gap. Cosign (part of the Sigstore project) signs images and stores the signature alongside them in the registry; consumers verify the signature before running, ensuring the image came from a trusted source and hasn't changed. Cosign supports keyless signing using short-lived certificates tied to an OIDC identity (e.g. your GitHub Actions workflow), so there's no long-lived private key to protect. In clusters, an admission controller (e.g. policy-controller / Kyverno) can enforce that only signed images from approved identities are allowed to run. Signing pairs naturally with SBOMs and provenance attestations for a verifiable build chain.

examples.label: Keyless sign in CI (OIDC identity)
examples.code:
cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp@sha256:abc123...
# Uses the workflow's OIDC identity; no key to manage

examples.label: Verify before deploy
examples.code:
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/eknatha/.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp@sha256:abc123...

examples.label: Enforce signatures in a cluster (conceptual)
examples.code:
# Sigstore policy-controller / Kyverno admission policy:
# reject images that aren't signed by an approved identity.

tips: Sign images in CI with keyless Cosign so there's no private key to leak.
Always sign and verify by digest (@sha256), not by mutable tag.
Enforce signature verification at the cluster admission layer for real protection.
gotchas: Signing by tag is meaningless if the tag can move — sign the digest.
Verification only helps if something actually enforces it; signing without an admission policy is advisory only.
Keyless signing depends on the OIDC issuer and identity matching — misconfigured identity regexes silently fail verification.

lessons.theory: Images are architecture-specific: an amd64 image won't run on an arm64 host (Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton, Raspberry Pi) and vice versa. docker buildx, backed by BuildKit, builds multi-platform images and publishes them as a single multi-arch manifest (a manifest list) — consumers automatically pull the variant matching their CPU. buildx builds for non-native architectures using QEMU emulation or remote/native builder nodes. You create a builder, then build with --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 and --push (multi-platform images must be pushed, not loaded into the local daemon, because the local store holds one architecture). This is essential now that ARM is everywhere in development and production.

examples.label: Set up and build multi-arch
examples.code:
docker buildx create --use --name multi
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp:1.0 \
  --push .

examples.label: Enable emulation for cross-builds
examples.code:
docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install all
# registers QEMU so x86 hosts can build arm64 and vice versa

examples.label: Inspect the manifest list
examples.code:
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp:1.0
# shows amd64 + arm64 variants under one tag

tips: Build linux/amd64,linux/arm64 so the same tag runs on Intel, Graviton, and Apple Silicon.
Multi-platform builds must --push (the local daemon can't hold multiple arches) — plan for a registry.
Use native builder nodes for speed; QEMU emulation works but is slower.
gotchas: 'exec format error' at runtime means an architecture mismatch — the wrong-arch image was pulled or built.
buildx multi-platform can't --load into the local daemon; only single-platform builds load locally.
Emulated cross-builds are much slower and occasionally hit emulation bugs in native code.

lessons.theory: Promotion is moving the exact same artifact through environments (dev → staging → prod) without rebuilding. The cardinal rule: build once, promote the same image by digest — never rebuild per environment, because a rebuild can produce different bytes (new base patches, dependency drift) and invalidate your testing. Practically, you build and tag with an immutable identifier (git SHA or semver), test that digest in staging, and then 'promote' by re-tagging or copying the same digest into the production repository (e.g. add a :prod or :stable tag, or copy across registries with a tool like crane/skopeo). Environment-specific configuration is injected at deploy time (env vars, config maps, secrets), not baked per environment. This guarantees that what you tested is byte-for-byte what you run.

examples.label: Promote by re-tagging the same digest
examples.code:
DIGEST=sha256:abc123...
# Promote the tested image to prod without rebuilding:
crane tag ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp@$DIGEST prod
# or copy across registries:
skopeo copy docker://ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp@$DIGEST \
             docker://prod-registry/myapp:stable

examples.label: Deploy references the digest, not :latest
examples.code: image: ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp@sha256:abc123...   # exact, tested bytes

examples.label: Config injected at deploy, not baked
examples.code:
# same image everywhere; only env/config differs per environment
environment:
  APP_ENV: production

tips: Build once, promote the same digest — never rebuild between staging and prod.
Use crane/skopeo to copy or re-tag images without pulling/pushing full layers.
Inject per-environment config at deploy time so one image serves all environments.
gotchas: Rebuilding per environment defeats the point — a fresh build may differ from what you tested.
Promoting a mutable :latest tag instead of a digest can deploy something other than what passed staging.
Baking environment config into the image forces per-env rebuilds and leaks config across stages.

lessons.theory: A typical containerised CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions checks out the code, sets up Buildx, logs in to a registry, then builds and pushes an image — increasingly via the official docker/build-push-action, which wraps Buildx with caching and multi-platform support. The pipeline is triggered on pushes/PRs and gates merges on tests. The build job should produce an immutable-tagged image (git SHA), run tests, scan for vulnerabilities, and only push on the right branches/tags. Using the maintained docker/* actions (setup-buildx-action, login-action, build-push-action, metadata-action) gives you caching, sensible tag generation, and provenance with little boilerplate. The output is a tested, tagged, scanned image in your registry, ready to deploy.

examples.label: Minimal build-and-push job
examples.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

examples.label: Auto-generate tags/labels
examples.code:
- id: meta
  uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
  with:
    images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
    tags: |
      type=sha
      type=semver,pattern={{version}}

examples.label: Gate push to main only
examples.code:
with:
  push: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}

tips: Use the official docker/* actions — they bring caching, tagging, and provenance for free.
Tag every build with the git SHA for traceability; add semver tags on releases.
Push only on protected branches/tags so PR builds don't publish images.
gotchas: Missing 'packages: write' permission makes the GHCR push fail with 403.
Forgetting cache config makes every CI build cold and slow.
Pushing on every PR pollutes the registry and can leak unreviewed images.

lessons.theory: CI runners are ephemeral, so the local layer cache that makes your laptop builds fast is empty on every run. The fix is external cache: BuildKit can export the build cache to a location and import it next time. With GitHub Actions the simplest backend is the built-in GitHub cache (type=gha); you can also use a registry as cache (type=registry, pushing a :cache tag) or inline cache embedded in the image. cache-to writes the cache after a build; cache-from seeds the next build from it. The payoff is large: dependency-install layers and other stable steps are restored instead of re-executed, cutting CI build times from minutes to seconds when only application code changed. mode=max caches all layers (including intermediate), not just the final ones.

examples.label: GitHub Actions cache backend
examples.code:
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    push: true
    tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

examples.label: Registry-backed cache (portable)
examples.code:
docker buildx build \
  --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/eknatha/app:buildcache \
  --cache-to   type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/eknatha/app:buildcache,mode=max \
  -t ghcr.io/eknatha/app:${GITHUB_SHA} --push .

examples.label: Keep the Dockerfile cache-friendly
examples.code:
COPY package*.json ./   # so the cached npm-ci layer is reused
RUN npm ci
COPY . .

tips: Use type=gha in GitHub Actions for zero-setup cross-run caching.
Use mode=max to cache intermediate layers, maximising reuse on later runs.
External cache only helps if your Dockerfile is ordered for caching (deps before source).
gotchas: Without external cache, ephemeral runners rebuild everything cold every time.
GitHub cache has size limits and eviction; very large caches get dropped and rebuild cold.
A poorly ordered Dockerfile gains little from caching — fix layer order first.

lessons.theory: Multi-stage builds aren't just for shrinking images — they're a clean way to run tests inside the build so a failing test fails the build and never ships. You add a test stage (FROM build AS test) that installs dev dependencies and runs the suite; if it exits non-zero, the docker build fails. The final runtime stage copies only production artifacts, so test frameworks and dev dependencies never reach the image. With Buildx you can build the test stage with --target test in CI and the runtime image separately, reusing cached layers. This keeps a single Dockerfile as the source of truth for build, test, and runtime, and guarantees the tested code and the shipped code came from the same build context.

examples.label: A test stage that gates the build
examples.code:
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM build AS test
RUN npm run lint && npm test   # build fails if tests fail

FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

examples.label: Run only the test stage in CI
examples.code: docker build --target test -t myapp:test .   # fails CI if tests fail

examples.label: Then build the runtime image
examples.code: docker build --target runtime -t myapp:${GITHUB_SHA} .

tips: Put lint/tests in a 'test' stage so a red suite fails the build before anything ships.
Keep test frameworks out of the runtime stage — copy only built artifacts forward.
Reuse cached build layers between the test and runtime targets to stay fast.
gotchas: If the test stage isn't actually built (wrong --target), tests silently don't run.
Tests needing a live database won't run inside the build — use Compose/services for those.
Copying from the wrong stage can pull dev dependencies into the runtime image.

lessons.theory: Vulnerability scanning belongs in the pipeline as an automated gate, not an afterthought. After building (and before or after pushing), run a scanner like Trivy against the freshly built image, configured to fail the job on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings. This stops known-vulnerable images from reaching production and surfaces issues while they're cheap to fix. Integrate results into the platform — for example, upload SARIF to GitHub so findings appear in the Security tab. Complement image scanning with dependency scanning (lockfiles), IaC/Dockerfile linting (hadolint), and secret scanning. Because new CVEs appear after an image is built, also scan images already in the registry on a schedule, not just at build time.

examples.label: Trivy gate in the pipeline
examples.code:
- uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
    severity: HIGH,CRITICAL
    ignore-unfixed: true
    exit-code: '1'        # fail the job on fixable high/critical CVEs

examples.label: Upload findings to GitHub Security tab
examples.code:
- uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
    format: sarif
    output: trivy.sarif
- uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
  with: { sarif_file: trivy.sarif }

examples.label: Lint the Dockerfile too
examples.code: docker run --rm -i hadolint/hadolint < Dockerfile

tips: Fail the build on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs; ignore unfixable ones to reduce noise.
Upload SARIF so vulnerabilities show up in code review and the Security tab.
Add hadolint (Dockerfile lint) and secret scanning alongside CVE scanning.
gotchas: Scanning only at build time misses CVEs disclosed later — schedule registry rescans.
Failing on unfixable CVEs blocks releases for issues you can't act on — filter them.
A scan gate without enforcement (continue-on-error: true) gives false confidence.

lessons.theory: Tags are how you find and deploy images, so a disciplined scheme is essential. Use immutable tags for anything you deploy: the git commit SHA (perfectly traceable to source) and/or semantic versions (1.4.2, plus moving 1.4 and 1 pointers on releases). Reserve mutable tags like :latest or :main for convenience only — never as a deployment reference, because they change and break rollbacks and audits. A common pattern: every build gets a :sha-<gitsha> tag; releases additionally get semver tags; environments are tracked by recording which digest is deployed, not by re-pointing a tag. docker/metadata-action can generate all of these automatically from git refs and tags. The principle: a deployed image must be identifiable back to an exact commit and an exact set of bytes.

examples.label: Auto-generate a tag matrix
examples.code:
- uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
  with:
    images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
    tags: |
      type=sha,prefix=sha-          # sha-abc1234 on every build
      type=ref,event=branch         # branch name for convenience
      type=semver,pattern={{version}}        # 1.4.2 on tag
      type=semver,pattern={{major}}.{{minor}} # 1.4 moving pointer

examples.label: Deploy by SHA or digest, not :latest
examples.code:
image: ghcr.io/eknatha/app:sha-abc1234
# or, most strictly, by digest:
image: ghcr.io/eknatha/app@sha256:...

examples.label: Tag a release
examples.code: git tag v1.4.2 && git push --tags   # triggers semver-tagged build

tips: Tag every build with the git SHA so any running image traces back to a commit.
Use semver tags for releases; keep :latest as convenience only, never for deploys.
Let docker/metadata-action generate the tag/label matrix from git context.
gotchas: Deploying :latest means two environments can run different code under one name — and rollbacks get ambiguous.
Re-using/moving a version tag breaks the immutability guarantee consumers rely on.
Without a SHA/semver tag, an incident becomes 'which commit is actually running?' guesswork.

lessons.theory: Once an image is in a registry, managed container platforms run it without you managing servers. AWS ECS (with Fargate) runs containers from a task definition that references the image, CPU/memory, env, and IAM role; you update the service to a new image and ECS performs a rolling deployment. Google Cloud Run runs a container as a stateless, autoscaling (including scale-to-zero) HTTP service — you deploy by pointing it at an image and it handles scaling and TLS. Azure Container Apps is the equivalent. The common deploy pattern from CI: build/push the image, then call the platform's deploy/update API/CLI with the new immutable tag or digest. These platforms expect stateless containers that read config from env/secrets and store state externally — exactly the twelve-factor shape Docker encourages.

examples.label: Deploy to Cloud Run from CI
examples.code:
gcloud run deploy myapp \
  --image ghcr.io/eknatha/myapp@sha256:abc123... \
  --region asia-south1 --platform managed \
  --set-env-vars APP_ENV=production --allow-unauthenticated

examples.label: Update an ECS service to a new image
examples.code:
aws ecs update-service --cluster prod \
  --service myapp --force-new-deployment
# (task definition references the new immutable image tag)

examples.label: Config via platform, not baked in image
examples.code:
# env vars and secrets supplied by the platform at deploy time
--set-env-vars LOG_LEVEL=info --set-secrets DB_PASS=db-pass:latest

tips: Deploy by immutable tag/digest so the platform runs exactly what you built and tested.
Keep containers stateless; let the platform inject config and secrets at deploy time.
Use the platform's rolling/blue-green deploys and health gates for zero-downtime releases.
gotchas: Deploying a mutable tag can make the platform pull something other than what you tested.
Scale-to-zero platforms (Cloud Run) add cold-start latency — size and warm accordingly.
Storing state on the container's local disk breaks on these platforms — containers are replaced freely.

lessons.theory: CI jobs that themselves build Docker images need access to a Docker engine. There are two patterns, and choosing wrong causes real problems. True Docker-in-Docker runs a nested dockerd inside the CI container (often the docker:dind service); it's isolated but requires --privileged, has storage-driver quirks, and a cold cache. The more common pattern is Docker-outside-of-Docker: mount the host's Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) into the CI container so it uses the host's engine — fast and cache-friendly, but the job effectively has root on the host, a serious security trade-off. Modern alternatives avoid a daemon entirely: BuildKit/buildx in rootless mode, or daemonless builders like Kaniko and Buildah, build images in CI without privileged DinD or socket mounting. Prefer these for untrusted or multi-tenant CI.

examples.label: DinD service (isolated, needs privileged)
examples.code:
services:
  docker:
    image: docker:25-dind
    privileged: true
# job talks to the dind daemon over tcp/socket

examples.label: Docker-outside-of-Docker (fast, risky)
examples.code:
docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  ci-image build-and-push.sh
# WARNING: this grants the job root-equivalent host access

examples.label: Daemonless build with Kaniko

tips: Prefer daemonless builders (Kaniko, Buildah) or rootless buildx for safer CI image builds.
If you must mount the Docker socket, understand it's root-equivalent host access and isolate the runner.
Use the host engine (socket) for cache speed only on trusted, single-tenant runners.
gotchas: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock gives the job full control of the host — a major privilege escalation in shared CI.
True DinD needs --privileged and can hit storage-driver/cache issues that slow or break builds.
Nested DinD cold caches make builds slow unless you wire up external cache.

lessons.theory: In production you must bound what each container can consume, or one misbehaving container can starve every other workload on the host (the 'noisy neighbour' problem). Docker exposes the kernel's cgroup controls: --memory sets a hard memory ceiling — exceed it and the kernel's OOM killer terminates the process — while --memory-reservation sets a soft target. --cpus limits CPU as a fraction of cores (--cpus=1.5 means 1.5 cores' worth), and --cpu-shares sets relative weighting under contention. The discipline that follows is requests vs limits: reserve what the app needs and cap what it may use. This concept carries directly into Kubernetes, where resources.requests drive scheduling (where a pod fits) and resources.limits enforce ceilings (and trigger OOMKills or CPU throttling). Always set both in production.

examples.label: Cap memory and CPU
examples.code:
docker run -d \
  --memory=512m --memory-reservation=256m \
  --cpus=1.5 \
  myapp
docker stats myapp   # watch live CPU/memory usage vs limits

examples.label: Compose resource limits
examples.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:   { cpus: '1.5', memory: 512M }
        reservations: { cpus: '0.5', memory: 256M }

examples.label: The same idea in Kubernetes
examples.code:
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi" }   # scheduling
  limits:   { cpu: "1500m", memory: "512Mi" }   # enforcement

tips: Always set memory and CPU limits in production to contain noisy neighbours.
Learn the requests-vs-limits split now — it's identical thinking to Kubernetes scheduling.
Use docker stats (or cAdvisor) to right-size limits from real usage rather than guessing.
gotchas: No --memory limit lets a leaking container consume all host RAM and take everything down.
Hitting the memory limit triggers an OOMKill (exit code 137) — looks like a crash but it's the cgroup ceiling.
CPU limits cause throttling, not killing — latency spikes under a too-tight --cpus are easy to misdiagnose.

lessons.theory: Production containers need to tell the platform whether they're actually working, and the platform needs a policy for what to do when they aren't. A Docker HEALTHCHECK (in the Dockerfile or compose) runs a command on an interval; the container's status becomes healthy or unhealthy, which orchestrators use to gate traffic and trigger replacement. Restart policies (--restart) decide automatic recovery: no (default), on-failure[:max] (restart only on non-zero exit, optionally bounded), always (restart even after a clean stop, and on daemon start), and unless-stopped (like always but respects a manual stop). The combination — a real healthcheck plus a sensible restart policy — gives you self-healing for transient failures. Kubernetes generalises this into liveness probes (restart if failing), readiness probes (remove from load balancing until ready), and startup probes (grace for slow boots).

examples.label: Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK
examples.code:
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 --start-period=20s \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

examples.label: Restart policy
examples.code:
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped --name api myapp
# survives crashes and daemon restarts, but honours a manual 'docker stop'

examples.label: Kubernetes probes (where this leads)
examples.code:
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 }, periodSeconds: 30 }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready,  port: 3000 }, periodSeconds: 10 }

tips: Expose a real /health endpoint that checks dependencies, not just 'process is up'.
Use unless-stopped for long-running services so they self-heal but respect manual stops.
Separate liveness (restart) from readiness (traffic gating) — they answer different questions.
gotchas: --restart always fights you during debugging by relentlessly restarting a crashing container.
A healthcheck that always returns 0 (or none at all) means the orchestrator can't tell a hung app from a healthy one.
A liveness probe that's really a readiness check (fails while a dependency is slow) causes needless restart loops.

lessons.theory: The twelve-factor rule for containers is: log to stdout/stderr and let the platform handle the stream — don't write log files inside the container, where they bloat the writable layer and vanish on removal. Docker captures stdout/stderr via a logging driver. The default json-file driver writes to host disk and, crucially, has no size cap by default, so it can fill the disk; always configure max-size and max-file rotation. Other drivers ship logs elsewhere: local (efficient default-ish), journald, syslog, fluentd, awslogs, gcplogs. In real systems you aggregate logs centrally — an agent (Fluent Bit, Vector, Promtail) tails container logs and forwards them to a backend (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Loki, CloudWatch) for search and alerting. Structured (JSON) logs make that pipeline far more useful than free-text lines.

examples.label: Cap json-file logs (prevent disk fill)
examples.code:
docker run -d \
  --log-driver json-file \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 \
  myapp

examples.label: Set rotation daemon-wide (daemon.json)
Ship to a backend (Compose, fluentd driver)
examples.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    logging:
      driver: fluentd
      options:
        fluentd-address: localhost:24224
        tag: app.{{.Name}}

tips: Log to stdout/stderr and let the platform collect it — never log to files inside the container.
Always set max-size/max-file on json-file logs, or disks fill silently.
Emit structured JSON logs so aggregation and querying actually work.
gotchas: Unbounded json-file logs are a classic 'disk full' production outage.
Writing logs to a file inside the container loses them on removal and bloats the writable layer.
Some logging drivers buffer or can block the container if the log backend is unreachable — pick and tune carefully.

lessons.theory: A single host running docker run or compose can't deliver production resilience: it can't reschedule containers when a node dies, scale services across machines, perform rolling updates with health gating, or self-heal. Orchestrators solve this. They run a control plane that holds your desired state and continuously reconciles the actual state toward it — if a container/pod dies or a node fails, the orchestrator recreates the workload elsewhere. Core capabilities across orchestrators: scheduling (placing workloads by resource requests and constraints), service discovery and load balancing, declarative rolling/blue-green deployments, horizontal autoscaling, secret/config management, and storage orchestration. Docker Swarm is the simple, Docker-native option; Kubernetes is the de-facto industry standard with a far richer ecosystem. The mental shift is from imperative ('start this container') to declarative ('keep N healthy replicas running, I don't care where').

examples.label: Declarative desired state (Kubernetes)
Docker Swarm (Docker-native orchestrator)
examples.code:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name api --replicas 3 -p 80:3000 myapp
docker service scale api=5         # self-healing, load-balanced

examples.label: Self-healing in action
examples.code:
# Kill a replica's container; the orchestrator notices the
# drift from desired state and starts a replacement automatically.

tips: Think declaratively: describe desired state and let the control plane reconcile to it.
Start with Swarm to grasp the concepts; invest in Kubernetes for the ecosystem and jobs.
Design stateless, health-reporting containers — orchestrators reschedule them freely.
gotchas: Lift-and-shifting stateful, non-health-reporting containers into an orchestrator gives little benefit and new failure modes.
Orchestration adds real operational complexity (networking, storage, control plane) — don't adopt it for a single small app.
Imperative habits (docker exec fixes on a node) get undone by the reconciler — change desired state instead.

lessons.theory: Compose and Kubernetes describe similar things with different vocabularies, so migration is largely a translation plus filling gaps Compose doesn't cover. A Compose service typically becomes a Deployment (for stateless apps) or StatefulSet (for stateful ones) plus a Service for stable networking; ports: that were published become a Service of type LoadBalancer/NodePort or an Ingress; environment: and env_file become ConfigMaps and Secrets; named volumes become PersistentVolumeClaims; depends_on disappears (Kubernetes has no start-order primitive — you rely on readiness probes and app retries); and deploy.replicas becomes the Deployment's replicas. Tools like Kompose can auto-generate a first draft of manifests, but treat their output as a starting point — production Kubernetes wants proper probes, resource requests/limits, labels/selectors, and security context that Compose never expressed. The migration is also a chance to add what Compose lacked: autoscaling, rolling-update strategy, and network policies.

examples.label: Compose service → Deployment + Service
examples.code:
# compose:  web: { image: myapp, ports: ['80:3000'] }
# becomes:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: myapp
        ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 3000 }]

examples.label: Auto-draft manifests with Kompose
examples.code:
kompose convert -f compose.yaml
# generates Deployment/Service YAML to refine (add probes, limits, etc.)

examples.label: Mappings cheat-sheet
examples.code:
# environment/env_file -> ConfigMap + Secret
# named volume        -> PersistentVolumeClaim
# depends_on          -> readiness probes + app retries (no direct equiv)
# deploy.replicas     -> Deployment.spec.replicas

tips: Map each Compose concept deliberately (service→Deployment+Service, volume→PVC, env→ConfigMap/Secret).
Use Kompose for a first draft, then add probes, resource requests/limits, and labels by hand.
Treat migration as an upgrade: add autoscaling, rolling strategy, and network policies Compose lacked.
gotchas: There's no depends_on in Kubernetes — relying on start order instead of readiness probes/retries breaks on day one.
Kompose output is a draft, not production-ready — missing probes, limits, and security context.
Compose's single flat network doesn't map to Kubernetes networking/Services — rethink connectivity, don't copy it.

lessons.theory: The closest Kubernetes analogue to a container is the Pod — but a Pod is not exactly a Compose service. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit and can hold one or more tightly-coupled containers that share a network namespace (same localhost and ports) and can share volumes — ideal for sidecars (a logging agent, a service-mesh proxy) that must live beside the main app. In Compose, by contrast, each service is its own isolated container reached by service name over the network; there's no shared-localhost grouping. You rarely create bare Pods in production; you let a controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job/CronJob) manage Pods for you so they're recreated and updated correctly. The other shift is configuration depth: a Pod spec carries probes, resource requests/limits, securityContext, volume mounts, and affinity rules — far more than a Compose service expresses — which is the surface the CKA exam tests heavily.

examples.label: A Pod with a sidecar (shared localhost)
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp
    ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
  - name: log-agent          # sidecar shares the Pod's network + volumes
    image: fluent/fluent-bit

examples.label: Compose equivalent has no shared localhost
Don't run bare Pods — use a controller
examples.code:
kind: Deployment   # manages Pods: recreation, rolling updates, scaling
# (also: StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob for other patterns)

tips: Use multi-container Pods only for tightly-coupled sidecars; otherwise one container per Pod.
Never deploy bare Pods in prod — wrap them in a Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet/Job.
Master the Pod spec fields (probes, resources, securityContext, volumes) — they're core CKA material.
gotchas: Treating a Pod like a whole Compose stack (cramming unrelated containers in) couples lifecycles that should be separate.
A bare Pod isn't recreated if it dies — only controllers give self-healing.
Containers in one Pod share localhost, so two of them can't bind the same port — unlike separate Compose services.

lessons.theory: Underneath Docker and Kubernetes sit lower-level runtimes, and understanding the layers demystifies a lot. There are two tiers: high-level runtimes (containerd, CRI-O) manage images, storage, and the container lifecycle and expose an API; low-level OCI runtimes (runc is the default; gVisor and Kata add stronger sandboxing) actually create the namespaces/cgroups and start the process. Docker uses containerd internally, which uses runc. Kubernetes talks to runtimes through the CRI (Container Runtime Interface). The widely-misunderstood 'Kubernetes is deprecating Docker' news (the dockershim removal) simply meant Kubernetes stopped using the Docker daemon as a middle layer and now talks to containerd (or CRI-O) directly — your Docker-built OCI images run exactly the same, because they conform to the OCI image spec. So 'Docker images' and 'containerd/CRI-O' are not competitors; they're different layers of one stack.

examples.label: The runtime stack
examples.code:
# Docker:      docker CLI -> dockerd -> containerd -> runc -> your process
# Kubernetes:  kubelet -> CRI -> containerd/CRI-O -> runc -> your process
# Same OCI image runs in both.

examples.label: Inspect containerd directly (ctr/crictl)
examples.code:
sudo ctr -n k8s.io images ls        # images containerd manages
sudo crictl ps                      # CRI-level view of running containers

examples.label: Sandboxed low-level runtime
examples.code:
# Use gVisor (runsc) for stronger isolation of untrusted workloads
docker run --runtime=runsc hostile-image

tips: Remember the layering: high-level runtime (containerd/CRI-O) on top of a low-level OCI runtime (runc).
Your Docker-built images are OCI images — they run unchanged on containerd/CRI-O under Kubernetes.
Learn ctr/crictl basics for debugging Kubernetes nodes where there's no Docker daemon.
gotchas: 'Kubernetes deprecated Docker' was about the dockershim, NOT about images — your images are unaffected.
On modern K8s nodes there's no Docker daemon, so 'docker ps' won't work — use crictl/ctr instead.
Swapping in a sandboxed runtime (gVisor/Kata) adds isolation but can break syscall-heavy or performance-sensitive workloads.

lessons.theory: The Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) is a hands-on, performance-based exam: you solve real tasks in live clusters from a terminal, not multiple-choice questions, so speed and kubectl fluency matter as much as knowledge. The current curriculum weights cluster architecture/installation, workloads & scheduling, services & networking, storage, and — heavily — troubleshooting. Everything in this DockerLab course is the on-ramp: containers, images, registries, networking, volumes, resource limits, healthchecks, and orchestration concepts all reappear as Kubernetes objects. Effective preparation is overwhelmingly practical: build muscle memory with kubectl, master kubectl explain and the official docs (allowed during the exam), set up imperative-command and alias shortcuts to save time, and drill troubleshooting. The CKA pairs naturally with the CKS (security) for engineers moving into platform/SRE roles, where Kubernetes operational depth is the differentiator.

examples.label: kubectl speed setup (do this first in the exam)
examples.code:
alias k=kubectl
export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'   # generate manifests fast
k run nginx --image=nginx $do > pod.yaml

examples.label: Imperative generation + explain (your best friends)
examples.code:
k create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3 $do > web.yaml
k explain deployment.spec.strategy   # the docs are available in-exam

examples.label: Troubleshooting drill (heavily tested)
examples.code:
k get pods -A | grep -v Running k describe pod

# events explain most failures k logs

--previous # last crash's logs k get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

tips: Practise in real clusters until kubectl is muscle memory — the CKA is timed and hands-on.
Lean on imperative commands + --dry-run=client -o yaml to scaffold manifests fast.
Drill troubleshooting hardest; describe + logs + events solve the majority of exam (and real) incidents.
gotchas: Trying to write every manifest by hand wastes precious exam time — generate then edit.
Neglecting troubleshooting practice hurts most: it's the largest, most time-pressured domain.
Memorising theory without terminal fluency fails a performance-based exam — practice beats reading.
